library/bit32.d:
This library provides functions to perform bitwise operations.

Number Limitations

This library treats numbers as unsigned 32-bit integers; numbers will be converted to this before being used (see image below). Numbers with decimal numbers are rounded to the nearest whole number.
library/bit32.s: A library of functions to perform bitwise operations.

m.d:
Returns the number x shifted disp bits to the right. The number disp may be any representable integer. Negative displacements shift to the left.

This shift operation is what is called arithmetic shift. Vacant bits on the left are filled with copies of the higher bit of x; vacant bits on the right are filled with zeros. In particular, displacements with absolute values higher than 31 result in zero or 0xFFFFFFFF (all original bits are shifted out).
m.s: Returns a number after its bits have been arithmetically shifted to the right by a given displacement.

p.s: The number whose bits shall be shifted.
The integer number of bits to shift by.

r.s: The result of arithmetically shifting x by disp bits to the right.

m.d:
Returns true if the bitwise AND of all its operands is different from zero, false otherwise. This is functionally equivalent to bit32.band(...) ~= 0 but returns a boolean directly without the intermediate number.

This function is useful for testing whether one or more specific bits are set in a value. For example, you can check whether a particular flag is active in a bitmask:

local flags = 0x5 -- bits 0 and 2 are set
print(bit32.btest(flags, 1)) --> true (bit 0 is set)
print(bit32.btest(flags, 2)) --> false (bit 1 is not set)
print(bit32.btest(flags, 4)) --> true (bit 2 is set)

When called with more than two arguments, all values are ANDed together before the zero-test:

print(bit32.btest(0xFF, 0x0F, 0x03)) --> true (0xFF & 0x0F & 0x03 == 0x03)
m.s: Returns a boolean describing whether the bitwise and of its operands is different from zero.

p.s: The numbers to test with bitwise AND.

r.s: True if the bitwise AND of all operands is non-zero, false otherwise.

Each bit is tested against the following truth table:

m.s: Returns the bitwise XOR of all provided numbers.

p.s: The numbers to combine with bitwise XOR.

r.s: The bitwise XOR of all provided numbers.

m.d:
Reverses the byte order of the 32-bit unsigned integer representation of x. The four bytes are rearranged so that the most-significant byte becomes the least-significant byte and vice versa, converting between big-endian and little-endian representations.

print(bit32.byteswap(0xAABBCCDD)) --> 0xDDCCBBAA
print(bit32.byteswap(0x00000001)) --> 0x01000000

This is useful when reading or writing binary data that uses a different byte order (endianness) than expected, such as network protocols or file formats that store multi-byte integers in big-endian order.
m.s: Returns the given number with the order of the bytes swapped.

p.s: The number whose bytes to swap.

r.s: The number with its byte order reversed.

m.d:
Returns the unsigned number formed by the bits field to field + width - 1 from n. Bits are numbered from 0 (least significant) to 31 (most significant). The default for width is 1.

For any valid field and width, this operation is equivalent to bit32.band(bit32.rshift(n, field), 2^width - 1). field must be in the range [0, 31], and width must be in the range [1, 32 - field]. Values outside those ranges raise an error.

local n = 0x12345678
assert(bit32.extract(n, 0, 8) == 0x78) -- bits 0 through 7
assert(bit32.extract(n, 4, 8) == 0x67) -- bits 4 through 11
assert(bit32.extract(n, 16, 8) == 0x34) -- bits 16 through 23
assert(bit32.extract(n, 24, 8) == 0x12) -- bits 24 through 31
m.s: Extract a range of bits from a number and return them as an unsigned number.

p.s: The number to extract bits from.
The zero-based position of the least significant bit to extract.
The number of bits to extract.

r.s: The unsigned number formed by the extracted bit range.

assert(bit32.lrotate(x, disp) == bit32.lrotate(x, disp % 32))

Returns the number x shifted disp bits to the left. The number disp may be any representable integer. Negative displacements shift to the right. In any direction, vacant bits are filled with zeros. For positive displacements, the following equality holds:

For any valid displacement, the following identity holds:

assert(bit32.rrotate(x, disp) == bit32.rrotate(x , disp % 32))

In particular, negative displacements rotate to the left.
m.s: Returns a number after its bits have been rotated to the right by a given number of times.

p.s: The number whose bits to rotate.
The number of bit positions to rotate right.

r.s: The result of rotating x right by disp bits.

m.d:
Returns the number x shifted disp bits to the right. The number disp may be any representable integer. Negative displacements shift to the left. In any direction, vacant bits are filled with zeros. In particular, displacements with absolute values higher than 31 result in zero (all bits are shifted out).

For positive displacements, the following equality holds:

assert(bit32.rshift(b, disp) == (b % 2^32 / 2^disp) // 1)

This shift operation is what is called logical shift.

library/buffer.d:
A buffer is an object that represents a fixed-size mutable block of memory. The buffer library provides functions for creation and manipulation of buffer objects, providing all its functions inside the global buffer variable.

Buffer is intended to be used a low-level binary data storage structure, replacing the uses of string.pack() and string.unpack(). Use cases include reading and writing existing binary formats, working with data in a more compact form, serialization to custom binary formats, and general work with native memory types like fixed-length integers and floats.

When passed through Roblox APIs, including sending a buffer through custom events, the identity of the buffer object is not preserved and the target will receive a copy. Similar to other limitations, the same buffer object cannot be used from multiple Actor scripts (Parallel Luau).

Many of the functions accept an offset in bytes from the start of the buffer. Offset of 0 from the start of the buffer memory block accesses the first byte. All offsets, counts and sizes should be non-negative integer numbers. If the bytes that are accessed by any read or write operation are outside the buffer memory, an error is thrown.

The read and write methods that work with integers and floats use little-endian encoding.

library/coroutine.d:
A coroutine is used to perform multiple tasks at the same time from within the same script. Such tasks might include producing values from inputs or performing work on a subroutine when solving a larger problem. A task doesn't even need to have a defined ending point, but it does need to define particular times at which it yields (pause) to let other things be worked on.

Using Coroutines

A new coroutine can be created by providing a function to coroutine.create(). Once created, a coroutine doesn't begin running until the first call to coroutine.resume() which passes the arguments to the function. This call returns when the function either halts or calls coroutine.yield() and, when this happens, coroutine.resume() returns either the values returned by the function, the values sent to coroutine.yield(), or an error message. If it does error, the second return value is the thrown error.

local function task(...)
    -- This function might do some work for a bit then yield some value
    coroutine.yield("first")  -- To be returned by coroutine.resume()
    -- The function continues once it is resumed again
    return "second"
end

local taskCoro = coroutine.create(task)
-- Call resume for the first time, which runs the function from the beginning
local success, result = coroutine.resume(taskCoro, ...)
print(success, result)  --> true, first (task called coroutine.yield())
-- Continue running the function until it yields or halts
success, result = coroutine.resume(taskCoro)
print(success, result)  --> true, second (task halted because it returned "second")

During the lifetime of the coroutine, you can call coroutine.status() to inspect its status:

Status Meaning
suspended The coroutine is waiting to be resumed. Coroutines begin in this state and enter it when their function calls coroutine.yield().
running The coroutine is running right now.
normal The coroutine is awaiting the yield of another coroutine; in other words, it has resumed another coroutine.
dead The function has halted (returned or thrown an error). The coroutine cannot be used further.

Wrapping Coroutines

When working with coroutines, you can also forgo the use of the coroutine object and instead use a wrapper function. Such a wrapper function will resume a particular coroutine when it is called and will return only the yielded values. You can do this using coroutine.wrap():

-- A simple coroutine body that returns a value
local function task()
    return "done"
end

-- Create coroutine and return a wrapper function that resumes it
local f = coroutine.wrap(task)
-- Resume the coroutine as if we called coroutine.resume()
local result = f()
print(result) --> done
-- If an error occurs it will be raised here!
-- This differs from coroutine.resume() which acts similar to pcall()

The first value returned from coroutine.resume() describes whether a coroutine ran without errors. However, functions returned by coroutine.wrap() will not do this: instead they directly return the values returned or passed to coroutine.yield(), if any. Should an error have occurred while running the coroutine function, the error is raised on the call of the returned function.

Producer Pattern Example

Imagine a task that produces repetitions of a word: each time it produces a repetition, the next one will produce one more. For example, providing Hello will produce Hello, HelloHello, HelloHelloHello, etc. To do this, you can define repeatThis():

-- This function repeats a word every time its coroutine is resumed
local function repeatThis(word)
    local repetition = ""
    while true do
        -- Do one repetition then yield the result
        repetition = repetition .. word
        coroutine.yield(repetition)
    end
end

To run this function as a coroutine, you can use coroutine.create() followed by multiple calls to coroutine.resume():

local function repeatThis(word)
    local repetition = ""
    while true do
        repetition = repetition .. word
        coroutine.yield(repetition)
    end
end

local repetitionCoro = coroutine.create(repeatThis)
print(coroutine.resume(repetitionCoro, "Hello"))  -- true, Hello
print(coroutine.resume(repetitionCoro))           -- true, HelloHello
print(coroutine.resume(repetitionCoro))           -- true, HelloHelloHello

For this producer function, you can also use coroutine.wrap() to get a function that produces values:

local function repeatThis(word)
    local repetition = ""
    while true do
        repetition = repetition .. word
        coroutine.yield(repetition)
    end
end

local f = coroutine.wrap(repeatThis)
print(f("Hello"))  -- Hello
print(f())         -- HelloHello
print(f())         -- HelloHelloHello
library/coroutine.s: A function that executes alongside the main thread.

m.d: Closes and puts the provided coroutine in a dead state. This function returns true unless the coroutine is in an error state, in which case it returns false and the error message. A coroutine that is currently running cannot be closed. A coroutine cannot be resumed after it is closed.
m.s: Closes and puts the provided coroutine in a dead state.

p.s: The coroutine thread to close.

r.s: true unless the coroutine being closed is in an error state.
The error message, if any.

kid.simple: Shuts a coroutine down for good (makes it dead) so it can never be resumed. Returns `true`, or `false` plus the error message if the coroutine had crashed.
kid.example:
local co = coroutine.create(function()
    coroutine.yield()
    print("never printed")
end)
coroutine.resume(co)   -- runs until the yield
coroutine.close(co)    -- close it while it is paused
print(coroutine.status(co)) -- dead
kid.gotcha: You cannot close a coroutine that is running right now.

m.d: Creates a new coroutine with body f, which must be a Luau function, and returns it as a thread. The returned coroutine starts in the suspended state and does not begin executing until coroutine.resume() is called on it. The arguments passed to the first coroutine.resume() call are forwarded as the arguments to f.
m.s: Creates a new coroutine, with body f. f must be a Luau function.

p.s: The Luau function to use as the coroutine body.

r.s: A new coroutine in the suspended state, ready to be resumed.

kid.simple: Turns a function into a new coroutine (a thread) that starts paused. Nothing runs until you call `coroutine.resume` on it. The values you pass to the first resume become the function's arguments.
kid.example:
local co = coroutine.create(function(a, b)
    print(a + b)
end)
coroutine.resume(co, 2, 3) -- prints 5

m.d:
Registers callback on coroutine co that will be called when co reaches a terminal state. The callback is called with a status string and a set of values:

  • callback("finished", ...results). The coroutine function returned. All result values are forwarded to the callback.
  • callback("error", err). The coroutine terminated with an error. The error value is passed as the only additional argument.
  • callback("cancelled"). coroutine.close() or task.cancel() was called on the coroutine. The coroutine did not complete its work. No extra values are provided.

Callbacks run at most once, in reverse registration order (LIFO).

When the coroutine reaches a terminal state during the invocation of coroutine.resume() or coroutine.close(), those functions will return only after callbacks complete their work. Callbacks are invoked on the calling thread and may yield. If a callback errors, remaining callbacks in the list are not invoked and false status with the callback error is returned.

Attempting to register a callback on a dead coroutine raises an error.

If a coroutine reaches a terminal state in a resume through coroutine.wrap() closure and has callbacks registered, it raises a "cannot run finalizers from a wrapped coroutine" error. A coroutine can also reach the terminal state when it is being resumed by the engine or closed with task.cancel(); in this case, callbacks are executed on a separate thread with errors reported as script errors.
m.s: Registers a callback to invoke when a coroutine finishes, errors, or is closed.

p.s: The coroutine thread to observe.
Function or a callable object to invoke.

kid.simple: Lets you attach a clean-up function that runs when a coroutine ends. Your function is told how it ended: "finished" (plus the returned values), "error" (plus the error), or "cancelled" (it was closed or cancelled early). Useful for tidying up no matter how the work ended.
kid.example:
local co = coroutine.create(function()
    coroutine.yield()
    return "treasure"
end)

coroutine.finally(co, function(status, ...)
    print("Coroutine ended:", status, ...)
end)

coroutine.resume(co) -- runs until the yield
coroutine.resume(co) -- prints: Coroutine ended: finished treasure
kid.gotcha: Adding a clean-up function to a coroutine that is already dead causes an error. Using it with a `coroutine.wrap` coroutine also errors when that coroutine ends.

m.d: Returns true if the coroutine this function is called within can safely yield. Yielding a coroutine inside metamethods or C functions is prohibited, with the exception of pcall and xpcall.
m.s: Returns `true` if the coroutine this function is called within can safely yield.

r.s: Whether or not the coroutine can safely yield at this point.

kid.simple: Returns true if the code running right now is allowed to pause (yield). Some special places, like inside metamethods, cannot pause.
kid.example: print(coroutine.isyieldable()) -- true in a normal script

m.d: Starts or continues the execution of coroutine co. The first time you resume a coroutine, it starts running its body. The values ... are passed as the arguments to the body function. If the coroutine has yielded, resume restarts it; the values ... are passed as the results from the yield. If the coroutine runs without any errors, resume returns true plus any values passed to yield (if the coroutine yields) or any values returned by the body function (if the coroutine terminates). If there is any error, resume returns false plus the error message.
m.s: Starts or continues the execution of coroutine `co`.

p.s: The coroutine thread to resume.
Arguments passed to the coroutine body function (on first resume) or returned from coroutine.yield() inside the coroutine (on subsequent resumes).

r.s: true if the coroutine ran without errors, false if an error occurred.
The values passed to coroutine.yield() or returned by the body function on success, or the error message on failure.

kid.simple: Starts a coroutine or continues it from where it last paused. It returns `true` plus any values from `yield` or `return` if all went well, or `false` plus an error message if the coroutine crashed.
kid.example:
local co = coroutine.create(function()
    error("oops!")
end)
local ok, message = coroutine.resume(co)
print(ok, message) -- false, followed by the error message containing oops!

m.d: Returns the currently running coroutine as a thread value, or nil if called from the main thread. The main thread is not considered a coroutine, so only threads created by coroutine.create() or coroutine.wrap() are returned by this function.
m.s: Returns the running coroutine.

r.s: The currently running coroutine, or nil if called from the main thread.

kid.simple: Gives you the thread that is running right now. Handy if you want to save it and resume it later from somewhere else.
kid.example:
local thread = coroutine.running()
print(thread) -- something like: thread: 0x...

m.d: Returns the status of coroutine co, as a string: 'running', if the coroutine is running (that is, it called status); 'suspended', if the coroutine is suspended in a call to yield, or if it has not started running yet; 'normal' if the coroutine is active but not running (that is, it has resumed another coroutine); and 'dead' if the coroutine has finished its body function, or if it has stopped with an error.
m.s: Returns the status of coroutine co as a string.

p.s: The coroutine thread to query.

r.s: One of "running", "suspended", "normal", or "dead".

kid.simple: Tells you what a coroutine is doing, as text: "suspended" (paused or not started), "running" (running right now), "normal" (it started another coroutine and is waiting on it), or "dead" (finished or crashed).
kid.example:
local co = coroutine.create(function() end)
print(coroutine.status(co)) -- suspended
coroutine.resume(co)
print(coroutine.status(co)) -- dead

m.d: Creates a new coroutine, with body f. f must be a Luau function. Returns a function that resumes the coroutine each time it is called. Any arguments passed to the function behave as the extra arguments to resume. Returns the same values returned by resume, except the first boolean. In case of error, propagates the error.
m.s: Creates a new coroutine and returns a function that, when called, resumes the coroutine.

p.s: The Luau function to use as the coroutine body.

r.s: A wrapper function that resumes the coroutine each time it is called, returning the yielded or returned values directly (without the boolean status). Raises an error if the coroutine errors.

kid.simple: Makes a coroutine and gives you back a normal function. Each time you call that function, the coroutine continues. It is shorter than create plus resume, and returns the values directly (without the true/false at the front).
kid.example:
local counter = coroutine.wrap(function()
    for i = 1, 3 do
        coroutine.yield(i)
    end
end)
print(counter(), counter(), counter()) -- 1 2 3
kid.gotcha: Errors inside a wrapped coroutine are NOT caught; they crash where you called it. Calling it again after it finished also errors.

m.d: Suspends the execution of the calling coroutine. Any arguments to yield are passed as extra results to resume. Yielding a coroutine inside metamethods or C functions is prohibited, with the exception of pcall and xpcall.
m.s: Suspends execution of the coroutine.

p.s: Values to return as additional results from the corresponding coroutine.resume() call.

r.s: The arguments passed to the next coroutine.resume() call that continues this coroutine.

kid.simple: Pauses the coroutine it is in. Any values you put in the parentheses are handed back to whoever resumed it. When it is resumed again, `yield` returns the values passed to that resume.
kid.example:
local co = coroutine.create(function()
    local answer = coroutine.yield("What is 2 + 2?")
    print("You said", answer)
end)

local _, question = coroutine.resume(co)
print(question)            -- What is 2 + 2?
coroutine.resume(co, 4)    -- You said 4

kid.simple: A coroutine is a function that can pause itself in the middle and be continued later, picking up exactly where it stopped. The coroutine library lets you make them, start or continue them, pause them, check on them, and close them. For most games, `task.spawn` is easier; coroutines are for when you want to control the pausing yourself.
kid.analogy: A coroutine is like reading a book with a bookmark. You read a few pages (run), put the bookmark in (yield), go do something else, then open the book and keep reading from the bookmark (resume).
whenToUse: Make a function that hands out values one at a time, like the next number in a list each time you ask
Split a big job into pieces that pause in between
Advanced control over threads that `task.spawn` alone does not give you
kid.where: A built-in library, so there is nothing to get. Works in any Script, LocalScript or ModuleScript on the server or client.

terms.coroutine: A function that can pause (yield) partway through and later continue from that same spot.
terms.thread: The value that represents a coroutine. `coroutine.create` gives you one. Your whole script is also running as a thread.
terms.yield: To pause. A coroutine yields with `coroutine.yield(...)`, and anything you put in the parentheses is handed back to whoever resumed it.
terms.resume: To start a coroutine, or continue it after it yielded.
terms.status: Which state a coroutine is in: `suspended` (paused or not started yet), `running` (running right now), `normal` (it started another coroutine and is waiting for it) or `dead` (finished or crashed).
terms.dead: Finished for good. A dead coroutine cannot be resumed again.
terms.callback: A function you give to something else so it can call it later.
terms.error: When code crashes because something went wrong. `coroutine.resume` catches errors and tells you about them instead of stopping your script.
terms.metamethod: A special advanced function on a table that runs automatically, for example when two tables are added. You cannot yield inside most of these.

examples.title: Pause and continue a coroutine
examples.code:
local co = coroutine.create(function(name)
    print("Hi " .. name)          -- runs on the first resume
    coroutine.yield("paused once") -- pause here and hand back a message
    print("Back again!")          -- runs on the second resume
    return "all done"
end)

print(coroutine.status(co))        -- suspended (made but not started)
print(coroutine.resume(co, "Sam")) -- Hi Sam, then: true paused once
print(coroutine.status(co))        -- suspended (paused at yield)
print(coroutine.resume(co))        -- Back again!, then: true all done
print(coroutine.status(co))        -- dead (finished)
explain: `coroutine.create` makes the coroutine but does not run it yet.
The first `resume` starts it and passes "Sam" in as `name`. It runs until `yield`.
`resume` gives back `true` (no error) plus whatever was passed to `yield`.
The second `resume` continues right after the yield line and runs to the end, giving back the return value.
Once it has finished, its status is `dead` and it cannot run again.

examples.title: A number machine with coroutine.wrap
examples.code:
-- each call gives the next even number
local nextEven = coroutine.wrap(function()
    local n = 0
    while true do
        n += 2
        coroutine.yield(n) -- hand back n and pause
    end
end)

print(nextEven()) -- 2
print(nextEven()) -- 4
print(nextEven()) -- 6
explain: `coroutine.wrap` makes a coroutine and gives you a plain function that resumes it.
Each time you call `nextEven()`, the loop runs once more, yields the new number, and pauses.
Its variable `n` is remembered between calls, because the coroutine is only paused, not finished. This endless loop is fine because it pauses at every yield.

gotchas: `coroutine.resume` catches errors: it returns `false` and the error message instead of crashing. Check the first value or you might miss bugs.
`coroutine.wrap` does NOT catch errors; an error inside it is thrown at the place you called it.
A dead coroutine cannot be resumed again. Make a new one instead.
For simply running code on the side, `task.spawn` is easier and works nicely with `task.wait`.
If a coroutine you control yields with `task.wait` inside, the game resumes it later on its own; mixing that with your own `coroutine.resume` calls gets confusing. Pick one style.

library/debug.d: Provides a few basic functions for debugging code in Roblox. Unlike the debug library found in Lua natively, this version has been heavily sandboxed.
library/debug.s: This library provides functions useful for debugging and profiling code.

m.d:
Returns a traceback of the current function call stack as a string; in other words, a description of the functions that have been called up to this point. During debugging, this behaves like an error stack trace but does not stop execution of the script.

The level parameter specifies what level of the call stack to consider, with 1 being the call of debug.traceback() itself, 2 being the call of the function calling debug.traceback(), and so on. See the code sample below for an example of sequential function calls.

Note that this function will often return inaccurate results (compared to the original source code) and that the format of the returned traceback may change at any time. You should not parse the return value for specific information such as script names or line numbers.

The following example includes sequential function calls; fnB() is called, and it calls fnA() which then calls debug.traceback().

local function fnA()
    print(debug.traceback("Specific moment during fnA()"))
end

local function fnB()
    fnA()
end

-- Call function fnB() to begin traceback
fnB()
m.s: Returns a string of undefined format that describes the current function call stack.

p.s: The first line of the returned string.
The number of calls "up" the call stack to return.

r.s: Traceback of the current function call stack.

m.d:
Allows programmatic inspection of the call stack. This function differs from debug.traceback() in that it guarantees the format of the data it returns. This is useful for general logging and filtering purposes as well as for sending the data to systems expecting structured input, such as crash aggregation.

local function fnA()
    -- Output source identifier ("s") and line ("l") at levels 1 and 2
    print(debug.info(1, "sl"))  --> fnA() 3
    print(debug.info(2, "sl"))  --> fnA() 7
end

fnA()

Note that this function is similar to debug.getinfo, an unavailable part of the standard Lua library which serves a similar purpose.
m.s: Traverses the entire stack of current thread and returns a string containing the call stack of target level details.

p.s: Determines at what level of the call stack the information returned should describe. A value of 1 represents the function which is calling debug.info(), a value of 2 represents the function that called that function, and so on.

A string that describes what the returned information should represent. It must only contain 0 or 1 instances of the characters slnaf, each representing a piece of information:

  • s (string) — The function source identifier, equal to the full name of the script the function is defined in.
  • l (number) — The line number of the function call represented by level.
  • n (string) — The name of the function; may be nil for anonymous functions and C functions without an assigned debug name.
  • a (number, boolean) — Arity of the function, which refers to the parameter count and whether the function is variadic.
  • f (function) — The function which was inspected.

r.s: One value per character in options, in the order they appear: source identifier (s), line number (l), function name (n), parameter count and whether variadic (a), or the function itself (f).

m.d: The value of Euler's number, e.
m.s: The value of Euler's number, e.

kid.simple: Euler's number, about 2.718. It shows up in growth and decay math. You will rarely need it in games.

m.d: Returns a value larger than or equal to any other numerical value (about 21024). Dividing a positive number by zero yields this same value.
m.s: Returns a value larger than or equal to any other numerical value (about 2<sup>1024</sup>).

kid.simple: A number bigger than any other number (infinity). Handy as a starting value when you are searching for the smallest distance.

local closestDistance = math.huge -- start with "infinitely far"
for _, part in workspace:GetChildren() do
	if part:IsA("BasePart") then
		local d = part.Position.Magnitude -- distance from (0, 0, 0)
		if d < closestDistance then
			closestDistance = d
		end
	end
end
print(closestDistance)

-- Spin a part one full turn
local part = workspace.Part
part.CFrame = part.CFrame * CFrame.Angles(0, math.tau, 0) -- ends where it started

print(math.deg(math.acos(0))) --> 90
local a = Vector3.new(1, 0, 0)
local b = Vector3.new(1, 1, 0).Unit
print(math.deg(math.acos(a:Dot(b)))) --> about 45

kid.example: print(math.deg(math.asin(1))) --> 90

kid.example: print(math.deg(math.atan(1))) --> 45  (a slope of 1 is a 45 degree hill)

p.s: The Y coordinate.
The X coordinate.

print(math.deg(math.atan2(1, -1))) --> 135

print(math.ceil(3.2))  --> 4
print(math.ceil(-3.8)) --> -3
-- How many buses of 30 seats for 95 kids?
print(math.ceil(95 / 30)) --> 4

print(math.clamp(-3, 0, 10)) --> 0

local part = workspace.Part
while true do
	local t = os.clock()
	part.Position = Vector3.new(math.cos(t) * 10, 5, math.sin(t) * 10)
	task.wait()
end

local broken = 0 / 0

m.d:
Returns a Perlin noise value. The returned value is most often between the range of -1 to 1 (inclusive) but sometimes may be outside that range; if the interval is critical to you, use math.clamp(noise, -1, 1) on the output.

If you leave arguments out, they will be interpreted as zero, so math.noise(1.158) is equivalent to math.noise(1.158, 0, 0) and math.noise(1.158, 5.723) is equivalent to math.noise(1.158, 5.723, 0).

Note that this function uses a Perlin noise algorithm to assign fixed values to coordinates. For example, math.noise(1.158, 5.723) will always return 0.48397532105446 and math.noise(1.158, 6) will always return 0.15315161645412.

If x, y, and z are all integers, the return value will be 0. For fractional values of x, y, and z, the return value will gradually fluctuate between -0.5 and 0.5. For coordinates that are close to each other, the return values will also be close to each other.

The noise repeats with a period of 256 on each axis, so math.noise(x, y, z) and math.noise(x + 256, y, z) return identical values.
m.s: Returns a Perlin noise value.

p.s: The X coordinate of the sample point.
The Y coordinate of the sample point.
The Z coordinate of the sample point.

r.s: A Perlin noise value, typically between -1 and 1.

kid.simple: Perlin noise: smooth randomness. Give it coordinates and it gives a number, usually between -1 and 1. Coordinates close together give values close together, so it looks natural, great for hills or gentle wobbling. The same inputs always give the same output. Whole-number inputs always give 0, so use decimals.
kid.example:
-- Build a row of bumpy hills
for x = 1, 50 do
	local height = math.noise(x / 10) * 20 + 25 -- divide by 10 so the hills are gentle
	local part = Instance.new("Part")
	part.Anchored = true
	part.Size = Vector3.new(4, height, 4)
	part.Position = Vector3.new(x * 4, height / 2, 0)
	part.Parent = workspace
end
kid.gotcha: `math.noise(1, 2, 3)` with whole numbers is always 0. Divide your inputs (like x / 10) so they are decimals.

For values like 0.5 that are equidistant to two integers, the value with the greater difference between it and zero is chosen. In other words, the function "rounds away from zero" such that 0.5 rounds to 1 and -0.5 rounds to -1.

kid.simple: Rounds to the nearest whole number. Exactly-halfway numbers go AWAY from zero, so 2.5 becomes 3 and -2.5 becomes -3.
kid.example:
print(math.round(5.8))  --> 6
print(math.round(5.2))  --> 5
print(math.round(2.5))  --> 3
print(math.round(-2.5)) --> -3

kid.example:
print(math.sign(-3)) --> -1
print(math.sign(0))  --> 0

print(math.sin(math.rad(90))) --> 1
print(math.sin(math.rad(30))) --> about 0.5

local light = workspace.Lamp.PointLight
while true do
	light.Brightness = 2 + math.sin(os.clock() * 3) -- goes between 1 and 3
	task.wait()
end
