kid.simple: `math` is a toolbox of number helpers that is always ready to use. It can round numbers, pick random numbers, keep a number inside a range, find the bigger of two numbers, and do angle math like sine and cosine. It also changes degrees into radians, which you need for CFrame rotations.
kid.analogy: `math` is like a calculator built into every script. You do not need to plug it in; just press its buttons, like `math.random` or `math.floor`.
whenToUse: Picking random things: `math.random(1, 6)` rolls a die.
Rounding: `math.floor`, `math.ceil`, `math.round`.
Keeping a value in a safe range: `math.clamp(health, 0, 100)`.
Converting angles: `math.rad(90)` for CFrame.Angles, `math.deg` to read angles back.
Smooth wavy motion with `math.sin` (bobbing coins, floating platforms).
Natural-looking random terrain or wobble with `math.noise`.
kid.where: A built-in library: works in every Script, LocalScript and ModuleScript. Just type `math.` and the function name. No game:GetService needed.

terms.library: A ready-made toolbox of functions you can use without making anything first.
terms.function: A named action you can call, like `math.floor(3.7)`. It takes values in and gives a value back.
terms.argument: A value you give to a function inside the brackets. In `math.max(3, 9)`, 3 and 9 are arguments.
terms.integer: A whole number with no decimal part, like 7 or -2.
terms.round down / floor: Go to the whole number just below (or equal): 3.7 becomes 3, and -3.2 becomes -4.
terms.round up / ceil: Go to the whole number just above (or equal): 3.2 becomes 4.
terms.absolute value: The number without its minus sign. The absolute value of -7 is 7.
terms.radians: The angle unit Roblox math uses. A full circle is 2 times pi radians (about 6.283), and 180 degrees is pi radians (about 3.1416). `math.rad` turns degrees into radians.
terms.pi: A special number, about 3.14159, that shows up whenever circles are involved.
terms.sine / cosine / tangent: Angle functions. If you walk around a circle, sine tells how high you are and cosine tells how far sideways. Both swing smoothly between -1 and 1, which is great for wavy motion.
terms.inverse trig (asin, acos, atan): The reverse of sine, cosine and tangent: you give a ratio and get back an angle in radians.
terms.clamp: Squash a number so it never goes below a minimum or above a maximum.
terms.lerp / interpolate: Find a number part-way between two numbers. Lerp from 0 to 10 with 0.5 gives 5.
terms.remainder: What is left over after dividing. 7 divided by 3 is 2 with 1 left over, so the remainder is 1.
terms.exponent / power: How many times to multiply a number by itself. 2 to the power 3 is 2*2*2 = 8.
terms.square root: The number that, multiplied by itself, gives the original. The square root of 16 is 4.
terms.logarithm: The reverse of a power: it asks "what power gives this number?". log base 2 of 8 is 3 because 2*2*2 = 8.
terms.infinity: A value bigger than every normal number. `math.huge` is Roblox's infinity.
terms.NaN: Short for Not a Number, a broken number you get from things like 0 divided by 0.
terms.pseudo-random: Numbers that look random but come from a recipe. The same seed always gives the same list.
terms.seed: The starting value for the random recipe. Same seed, same "random" numbers.
terms.Perlin noise: A kind of smooth randomness: nearby inputs give nearby outputs, so it looks natural, like rolling hills instead of spiky static.
terms.hyperbolic functions (sinh, cosh, tanh): Advanced cousins of sin, cos and tan used in special curves. Most games never need them.
terms.mantissa: In `math.frexp`, the "main digits" part of a number when it is written as mantissa times 2 to some power.

examples.title: Roll a die
examples.code:
local roll = math.random(1, 6) -- a whole number from 1 to 6
print("You rolled a " .. roll)

if roll == 6 then
	print("Lucky six!")
end
explain: `math.random(1, 6)` picks a whole number from 1 up to 6, and both ends can be picked.
Each time the script runs you get a new roll.

examples.title: Keep health between 0 and 100
examples.code:
local health = 80

health = health + 50                 -- now 130, too much!
health = math.clamp(health, 0, 100)  -- squash it back into range
print(health) --> 100

health = health - 250                -- now -150
health = math.clamp(health, 0, 100)
print(health) --> 0
explain: `math.clamp(x, min, max)` returns x, unless it is below min (then min) or above max (then max).

examples.title: Make a coin bob up and down
examples.place: Script inside an Anchored Part (the coin) in Workspace
examples.code:
local coin = script.Parent
local startPosition = coin.Position

while true do
	-- math.sin swings smoothly between -1 and 1 as time goes on
	local height = math.sin(os.clock() * 2) * 1.5
	-- Also spin it: os.clock() grows every second, math.rad turns degrees into radians
	local spin = CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(os.clock() * 90), 0)
	coin.CFrame = CFrame.new(startPosition + Vector3.new(0, height, 0)) * spin
	task.wait()
end
explain: `os.clock()` is a timer that keeps counting up in seconds.
`math.sin` of a growing number goes up and down between -1 and 1 forever, like a wave.
Multiplying by 1.5 makes the coin move 1.5 studs up and 1.5 studs down.
`math.rad(os.clock() * 90)` spins it 90 degrees every second, converted to radians for CFrame.Angles.

gotchas: Trig functions (sin, cos, tan) use radians, not degrees. `math.sin(90)` is NOT 1; `math.sin(math.rad(90))` is.
`math.random(1, 6)` gives whole numbers, but `math.random()` with no arguments gives a decimal from 0 up to (but not including) 1.
`math.floor(-3.2)` is -4, not -3. Floor always goes DOWN, even for negative numbers.
You cannot check for NaN with `==`. `math.nan == math.nan` is false. Use `math.isnan`.
In `math.clamp`, the max must be greater than or equal to the min, or you get an error.
For more control over randomness (for example, several separate random streams), Roblox also has the `Random` data type.

library/os.d: This library currently serves the purpose of providing information about the system time under the UTC format. It has been heavily sandboxed from the standard Lua os library and does not allow you to perform any system-altering operations.
library/os.s: This library provides functions related to time and date.

m.d:
Returns elapsed time in seconds since an arbitrary baseline with sub-microsecond precision. This function is useful for comparing durations between two events that occur on the same computer, and is the best option for benchmarking.

Unlike with functions such as os.time() or DateTime.now(), adjustments to the system clock (such as by the user or NTP) do not cause time to jump forwards or backwards.

-- Record the initial time:
local startTime = os.clock()
-- Do something you want to measure the performance of:
local a, b = 0, 1
for _ = 1, 5000000 do
    a, b = b, a
end
-- Measure amount of time this took:
local deltaTime = os.clock() - startTime
print("Elapsed time: " .. deltaTime)
-->  Elapsed time: 0.044425600033719 (actual number may vary)
m.s: Returns elapsed time in seconds since an arbitrary baseline with sub-microsecond precision.

m.d:
Formats the given formatString with date/time information based on the given time, or if not provided, the value returned by os.time().

This function should be avoided in new work. Instead, use the DateTime API, which supports localized formatting.

The following specifiers (based on the C function strftime) are supported:

Specifier Meaning Example†
%a Abbreviated weekday name * Mon
%A Full weekday name * Monday
%b Abbreviated month name * Feb
%B Full month name * February
%c Date and time * Mon Feb 12 14:14:35 2024
%d Day of the month 12
%H Hour, using 24-hour clock 14
%I Hour, using 12-hour clock 02
%j Day of year 043
%m Month 02
%M Minute 14
%p Either "AM" or "PM" PM
%S Second 35
%U Week number (first Sunday as the first day of week one) 06
%w Weekday 1
%W Week number (first Monday as the first day of week one) 07
%x Date * 02/12/24
%X Time * 14:14:35
%y Two-digit year 24
%Y Full year 2024
%z ISO 8601 offset from UTC in timezone (1 minute = 1, 1 hour = 100) -0800
%Z Timezone name or abbreviation * PST
%% The % character %

* This value can vary depending on the current locale.

† The example provided is for February 12th, 2024 (Monday) at 2:14:35 PM (14:14:35), run using locale "en-us" in Pacific Standard Time (PST).

If the provided formatString is exactly "*t" (local time) or "!*t" (UTC time), this function instead returns a dictionary containing the following components, which are normally available in the specifiers above.

Field Type Description
year int An integer that describes the current year of the Current Era (ex. 2017)
month int An integer between 1 and 12 (starting from January) that describes the current month.
wday int An integer between 1 and 7 (starting from Sunday) that describes the current week day.
yday int An integer between 1 and 366 describing how many days we are into the year.
There can be 366 days if it is a leap year.
day int An integer between 1 and 31 describing the current day of the month.
hour int An integer between 1 and 24 describing the current hour of the day.
min int An integer between 0 and 59 describing the current minute of the hour.
sec int An integer between 0 and 60 describing the current second of the hour.
(60 because the function is described to indicate leap seconds, but in practice it probably doesn't).
isdst bool A boolean describing if daylight savings time is currently active.
m.s: Formats the given string with date/time information based on the given time.

p.s: Must be either "*t" or "!*t".
The time value to format.

m.d: Returns the number of seconds from t1 to t2. The difference is computed assuming that t1 and t2 are correctly casted to the time_t format.
m.s: Returns the number of seconds from one time to another.

p.s: The later time value, as returned by os.time().
The earlier time value, as returned by os.time().

m.d:
Returns how many seconds have passed since the Unix epoch (1 January 1970, 00:00:00), under current UTC time. If provided a table formatted similarly to that returned by os.date(), it returns the number of seconds from the Unix epoch to that time instead.

Note that the returned time uses the device's local clock. Most operating systems automatically sync their local time against online time servers, so this should be within a few hundred milliseconds. However, users can easily disable sync behavior and set the system time to anything they want; for synchronized time between client and server, use Workspace:GetServerTimeNow() instead.

This function should be avoided in new work. Instead, use the DateTime API, which supports localized formatting.

When you need to precisely measure the time elapsed between two points in time, like when testing performance, use os.clock() instead.
m.s: Returns how many seconds have passed since the Unix epoch (1 January 1970, 00:00:00) under current UTC time.

p.s: A dictionary table describing a specific time, similar to that returned by os.date(). If not provided, uses the current UTC time.

library/string.d:
The string library provides generic functions to manipulate strings, such as to extract substrings or match patterns. You can access the string library by the global string library.

See String pattern reference for details on using string.match(), string.gmatch(), and string.gsub() to find (and replace) substrings.
library/string.s: Provides generic functions to manipulate strings.

m.d:
Returns the internal numerical codes of the characters s[i], s[i+1], ..., s[j]. The default value for i is 1; the default value for j is i. These indices are corrected following the same rules of function string.sub().

Numerical codes correspond to single-byte character values (0-255). The function returns one number per character in the specified range, so calling it on a multi-character slice yields multiple return values. If the resolved range is empty (start index greater than end index after adjustment), no values are returned.

-- Single character
print(string.byte("A")) -- 65

-- Range of characters
print(string.byte("hello", 1, 3)) -- 104 101 108

-- Negative indices (counts from end)
print(string.byte("abc", -1)) -- 99 (the byte value of 'c')

-- Roundtrip with string.char
local a, b, c = string.byte("ABC", 1, 3)
print(string.char(a, b, c)) -- ABC
m.s: Returns the internal numerical codes of the characters `s[i], s[i+1], ..., s[j]`. The default value for `i` is `1`; the default value for `j` is `i`. These indices are corrected following the same rules of function string.sub.

p.s: The string to extract byte values from.
The starting index of the range of characters to convert.
The ending index of the range of characters to convert.

kid.simple: Gives the number code (byte) for a character, or several characters. "A" is 65, "a" is 97. The opposite of `string.char`.
kid.example:
print(string.byte("A"))        -- 65
print(string.byte("Hi", 1, 2))  -- 72 105

m.d:
Receives zero or more integers and returns a string with length equal to the number of arguments, in which each character has the internal numerical code equal to its corresponding argument.

Each integer must be in the range [0, 255]; values outside that range raise an error. This is the inverse of string.byte().

-- Basic usage
print(string.char(72, 101, 108, 108, 111)) -- Hello

-- Single character
print(string.char(65)) -- A

-- Construct from byte values (e.g. null byte)
local s = string.char(0)
print(#s) -- 1

-- Roundtrip with string.byte
local code = string.byte("Z")
print(string.char(code)) -- Z
m.s: Receives zero or more integers and returns a string with length equal to the number of arguments, in which each character has the internal numerical code equal to its corresponding argument.

p.s: Zero or more integers in the range [0, 255], each representing a byte value.

kid.simple: Builds a string from number codes (0 to 255). The opposite of `string.byte`.
kid.example: print(string.char(72, 105)) -- Hi
kid.gotcha: Numbers outside 0 to 255 cause an error.

m.d:
Searches for the first occurrence of a pattern in a string and returns the start and end indices of the match. If no match is found, it returns nil. You can specify where to start the search using the optional init parameter which defaults to 1 and can be negative. An optional plain parameter turns off pattern matching, so the function performs a plain substring search; note that if you use plain, you must also provide init.

-- Example 1: Basic usage
local s = "Hello, world!"
local pattern = "world"
local start_index, end_index = string.find(s, pattern)
print(start_index, end_index)  -- Output: 8 12

-- Example 2: Using init parameter
local s = "Hello, world! Hello, Roblox!"
local pattern = "Hello"
local start_index, end_index = string.find(s, pattern, 10)
print(start_index, end_index)  -- Output: 15 19

-- Example 3: Using plain parameter
local s = "Hello, world! (Hello)"
local pattern = "(Hello)"
local start_index, end_index = string.find(s, pattern, 1, true)
print(start_index, end_index)  -- Output: 14 20

-- Example 4: No Pattern found
local s = "Hello, world!"
local pattern = "Roblox"
local start_index, end_index = string.find(s, pattern)
print(start_index, end_index)  -- Output: nil
m.s: Looks for the first match of pattern in the string `s` and returns the indices of `s` where the occurrence starts and ends.

p.s: The string to search within.
The pattern to search for in given string.
The starting index for the search.
If true, turns off pattern matching and performs a plain substring search.

r.s: The starting index of the match.
The ending index of the match.

kid.simple: Searches for some text (or a pattern) and gives back the start and end positions of the first match, or nil if it is not found. An optional 3rd value says where to start; a 4th value of true means "search for these exact characters, no pattern codes".
kid.example:
local s = "Hello, world!"
print(string.find(s, "world"))      -- 8 12
print(string.find(s, "pizza"))      -- nil
print(string.find("a.b", ".", 1, true)) -- 2 2 (a real dot, not "any character")
kid.gotcha: Without `plain = true`, a `.` means "any character", so `string.find("abc", ".")` finds position 1.

m.d:
Returns a formatted version of its variable number of arguments following the description given in its first argument, which must be a string.

You can convert variables into user-friendly strings of text using the string.format() function. The function requires the following format:

%[flags][width].[precision][specifier].

Specifiers

The most important part of string formatting is the specifiers.

Specifier Accepts Outputs Example Output
c integer 3
d or i integer Decimal representation. 321
e or E float Scientific notation using e or E. 3.296e2
3.296E2
f float 3231.1231
g or G float The shorter of e/E and f. 3E14
3e14
o integer Octal representation. 610
q string String in a form suitable to be safely read back by the Luau interpreter. The string is written between double quotes and all double quotes, new lines, embedded zeros, and backslashes are correctly escaped. "print(\"Hi\")"
s string Hello world!
u integer Decimal representation. 3131
x or X integer Hexadecimal representation. 7fa
7FA
* any Equivalent to s but accepts any variable by converting it to a string using Global.LuaGlobals.tostring(). table: 0x0123456789abcdef
% % followed by another % will return the % sign itself. % 
local str = "The magic word is %s"
print(string.format(str, "Roblox"))
-- The magic word is Roblox

local str = "The magic word is %q"
print(string.format(str, "Roblox"))
-- The magic word is "Roblox"

local str = "Skip to \na new line and \nanother new line!"
print(string.format(str, "%q"))
--[[ Output:
Skip to
a new line and
another new line!
]]

Flags

Flag Description
- Left-justify the given field width (see Width below). Right justification is the default.
+ Forces a + sign to precede a number. Has no effect on negative numbers.
(space) One blank space is inserted before a positive number, while negative numbers are unaffected. This is useful for making positive and negative numbers vertically align in a visual stacked list.
# When used with o and x/X, writes a 0 (octal) or 0x/0X (hex) before values other than zero.
When used with e/E and f, forces the output to contain a decimal point, even if no digits would follow (by default, no decimal point is written if no digits follow).
When used with g or G, the result is the same as with e or E but trailing zeros are not removed.
0 Left-pads the number with zeros instead of empty spaces (see Width below). 
local str = "%-10d"
print(string.format(str, 300) .. "]")
-- 300       ]
-- There are 7 spaces between '300' and ']'

local str = "%+i versus %+i"
print(string.format(str, 300, -300)) -- +300 versus -300

local str = "There is a% i%% chance of rain in Seattle today."
print(string.format(str, 100))
-- There is a 100% chance of rain in Seattle today.

Width

Width Description
(number) Minimum number of characters to return. If the number of characters to be formatted is less than this number, the result is padded with blank spaces. 
local str = "%012i"
print("Score: " .. string.format(str, 15000))
-- Output: Score: 000000015000
-- The output has 12 digits total, left-padded with zeros

Precision

The default precision is 1. If you give a period without a value, the default is 0.

Precision Description
.(number) For integer specifiers (d, i, o, u, x/X), precision specifies the minimum number of digits to be returned. If the value to be formatted is shorter than this number, the result is padded with leading zeros. A precision of 0 means that no character is written for the value 0.
For e/E and f specifiers, this is the number of digits to be printed after the decimal point.
For g/G specifiers, this is the maximum number of digits (before the e/E, if present).
For s, this is the maximum number of characters to be returned.
For c and q, this has no effect.		 
-- Add decimal with precision of 2 for a currency output
local str = "$%.2f"
print(string.format(str, 300)) -- Output: $300.00

-- Return first 6 letters of a string
local str = "%.6s"
print(string.format(str, "Robloxian")) -- Output: Roblox

local str = "Once upon a time, there was a dragon named %s and it had %.8f horns."
print(string.format(str, "Pi", math.pi))
-- Output: Once upon a time, there was a dragon named Pi and it had 3.14159265 horns.
m.s: Returns a formatted version of its variable number of arguments following the description given in its first argument, which must be a string.

p.s: A string containing format specifiers that control how subsequent arguments are formatted.
Values to be formatted according to the specifiers in the format string.

kid.simple: Builds text from a template with slots. `%d` = whole number, `%s` = text, `%.2f` = decimal with 2 digits after the dot, `%02d` = pad with zeros to 2 digits, `%x` = hexadecimal, `%%` = a real percent sign.
kid.example:
print(string.format("Level %d", 5))           -- Level 5
print(string.format("Price: %.2f", 3.5))      -- Price: 3.50
print(string.format("%s scored %d", "Mia", 9)) -- Mia scored 9

m.d:
Returns an iterator function that, each time it is called, returns the next captures from pattern over the string s. If the pattern has no captures, the whole match is returned on each call.

The iterator is typically used in a generic for loop. When the pattern contains capture groups, each call returns the captured substrings as separate values. An empty match (zero-width) advances past the current position by one character to avoid an infinite loop.

-- Iterate over all words in a sentence
for word in string.gmatch("Hello Roblox world", "%a+") do
    print(word)
end
-- Hello
-- Roblox
-- world

-- Extract key-value pairs using captures
local t = {}
for key, value in string.gmatch("name=Roblox, version=1.0", "(%w+)=(%w[%w.]*)") do
    t[key] = value
end
print(t.name, t.version) -- Roblox 1.0

-- Collect all digits
local digits = {}
for d in string.gmatch("abc123def456", "%d+") do
    table.insert(digits, d)
end
print(table.concat(digits, ", ")) -- 123, 456
m.s: Returns an iterator function that returns the next captures from pattern over the string `s` each time it's called.

p.s: The string to search for pattern matches.
The pattern to match repeatedly against the string.

kid.simple: Lets you loop over every match of a pattern in a string, one at a time, using a `for` loop.
kid.example:
for word in string.gmatch("Hello Roblox world", "%a+") do
    print(word) -- Hello, then Roblox, then world
end

m.d:
Short for global substitution. Returns a copy of s in which all (or the first n, if given) occurrences of the pattern are substituted (replaced) with the given replacement. The second value returned is the total number of substitutions made.

The replacement can be one of several types, each used differently to determine the actual string:

  • string: The pattern is replaced with the string directly
  • table: The string that matched the pattern is looked up in the table as a key, and the value (string) is what replaces it, if it exists.
  • function: Called with the string that matched the pattern, should return the string to replace the matched pattern.

An optional final argument can be provided which specifies the maximum number of substitutions to make (for example, stop after 2 replacements)

Various Examples

-- Basic replacement
string.gsub("I love tacos!", "tacos", "Roblox") --> I love Roblox! 1
-- Replacement with a pattern
string.gsub("I like red!", "%w+", "word") --> word word word! 3
-- Replacement table
string.gsub("I play Roblox.", "%w+", {I="Je", play="joue à"}) --> "Je joue à Roblox." 3
-- Replacement function
string.gsub("I have 2 cats.", "%d+", function(n) return tonumber(n) * 12 end) --> "I have 24 cats." 1
-- Replace only twice
string.gsub("aaa", "a", "b", 2) --> "bba" 2
-- Replacement with capture groups (maximum of nine)
string.gsub("love2play Roblox", "(%w+)(%d+)(%w+)%s+(%w+)", "I %1 %2 %3 %4!") --> "I love 2 play Roblox!" 1
m.s: Returns a copy of `s` in which all or the first `n` occurrences of the pattern are replaced with the given replacement. The second value returned is the total number of substitutions made.

p.s: The string whose occurrences of the given pattern shall be replaced.
The pattern to be matched and replaced.
Determines what should replace the occurrence(s) of the given pattern.
The maximum number of substitutions to make.

kid.simple: Replaces every match of a pattern with something else, and gives back the new string plus how many replacements it made. The replacement can be text, a table, or a function. An optional 4th number limits how many to replace.
kid.example:
local newText, count = string.gsub("I like cats and cats", "cats", "dogs")
print(newText) -- I like dogs and dogs
print(count)   -- 2
kid.gotcha: It returns TWO values. If you put it straight into another function call, the count goes in too; wrap it in parentheses `(string.gsub(...))` to keep only the text.

m.d:
Returns the number of bytes in the string s. Because Luau strings are byte sequences, this counts bytes rather than Unicode characters or grapheme clusters. An empty string returns 0. Embedded null bytes (\0) are included in the count.

print(string.len("Hello")) -- 5
print(string.len(""))      -- 0

-- Embedded null bytes are counted
local s = "ab\0cd"
print(string.len(s)) -- 5

-- Equivalent to the # length operator
local str = "Roblox"
print(string.len(str) == #str) -- true
m.s: Returns the length of a string.

p.s: The string to measure.

kid.simple: Counts how many bytes are in a string, which for normal English text is the number of characters. Same as writing `#text`.
kid.example:
print(string.len("Roblox")) -- 6
print(#"Roblox")           -- 6, the same thing

m.d:
Returns a copy of the string s with all uppercase ASCII letters (A-Z) changed to their lowercase equivalents (a-z). Characters outside the ASCII letter range, including accented or multibyte characters, are left unchanged.

print(string.lower("HELLO")) -- hello
print(string.lower("Hello World!")) -- hello world!

-- Non-letter characters are unaffected
print(string.lower("Roblox 123!")) -- roblox 123!

-- Only ASCII letters are converted
print(string.lower("ABC abc")) -- abc abc
m.s: Returns a copy of a string with all uppercase letters changed to lowercase.

p.s: The string to convert to lowercase.

kid.simple: Gives back a copy with all A to Z letters made lowercase. Great for comparing text without caring about capitals.
kid.example:
print(string.lower("HeLLo")) -- hello
if string.lower("YES") == "yes" then print("match") end

m.d:
Looks for the first match of pattern in the string s. If the pattern contains captures, the captured substrings are returned as separate values; otherwise, the whole match is returned. If no match is found, the function returns nil.

The optional third argument init specifies the byte position to start the search (default 1). A negative init counts from the end of the string. Unlike string.find(), this function returns captured values directly rather than the match indices.

-- Extract matched substring
print(string.match("I have 42 cats", "%d+")) -- 42

-- Multiple captures
local year, month, day = string.match("2024-03-15", "(%d+)-(%d+)-(%d+)")
print(year, month, day) -- 2024 03 15

-- No match returns nil
print(string.match("hello", "%d+")) -- nil

-- Using init to skip ahead
print(string.match("foo123bar456", "%d+", 7)) -- 456

-- Anchored pattern
print(string.match("hello", "^%a+")) -- hello
m.s: Looks for the first match of `pattern` in the string `s`.

p.s: The string to search for a pattern match.
The pattern to match against the string.
The byte position at which to start searching.

kid.simple: Finds the first part of a string that matches a pattern and gives it back (or nil). If the pattern has captures in ( ), it gives back just those parts.
kid.example:
print(string.match("I have 42 cats", "%d+"))   -- 42
local name, age = string.match("Sam:12", "(%a+):(%d+)")
print(name, age) -- Sam 12

m.d: Returns a binary string containing the provided arguments. The first argument, format, determines the way the remaining arguments are packed; see here for options.
m.s: Returns a binary string containing the provided arguments.

p.s: A format string that describes the layout and types of the values to pack.
The values to serialize into binary form according to the format string.

kid.simple: Advanced. Squeezes numbers and text into a compact binary string using a format code, for saving space. Use `string.unpack` to read it back.
kid.example:
local packed = string.pack("i4", 1000) -- a 4-byte whole number
print(#packed) -- 4

m.d: Returns the size in bytes of any string packed with a given description. The sole argument, format, determines the way the remaining arguments are packed, but you cannot use s and z because they have variable lengths. See here for options.
m.s: Returns the size in bytes of any string packed with a given description.

p.s: A format string describing the packing layout (must not contain variable-length options s or z).

kid.simple: Advanced. Tells you how many bytes `string.pack` will use for a format.
kid.example: print(string.packsize("i4i4")) -- 8

m.d:
Returns a string that is the concatenation of n copies of the string s. If n is zero or negative, the function returns an empty string. An error is raised if the resulting string would exceed the maximum string size.

print(string.rep("ab", 3))  -- ababab
print(string.rep("Go! ", 2)) -- Go! Go!

-- Zero or negative repeats return empty string
print(string.rep("x", 0))  -- (empty string)
print(string.rep("x", -1)) -- (empty string)

-- Useful for padding or separators
local separator = string.rep("-", 20)
print(separator) -- --------------------
m.s: Returns a string that is the concatenation of `n` copies of the string `s`.

p.s: The string to repeat.
The number of times to repeat the string.

kid.simple: Repeats a string a number of times. 0 or less gives an empty string.
kid.example:
print(string.rep("ha", 3))  -- hahaha
print(string.rep("-", 10))  -- ----------

m.d:
Returns a string that is the string s reversed byte-by-byte. Because the reversal operates on individual bytes, multibyte UTF-8 sequences are not preserved as valid characters after reversal.

print(string.reverse("hello"))  -- olleh
print(string.reverse("Roblox")) -- xolboR

-- Single character or empty string
print(string.reverse("a")) -- a
print(string.reverse(""))  -- (empty string)

-- Palindrome check
local function isPalindrome(s)
    local lower = string.lower(s)
    return lower == string.reverse(lower)
end
print(isPalindrome("racecar")) -- true
print(isPalindrome("hello"))   -- false
m.s: Returns a string that is the string `s` reversed.

p.s: The string to reverse.

kid.simple: Gives back the string backwards.
kid.example: print(string.reverse("Roblox")) -- xolboR

m.d:
Splits a string into parts based on the defined separator character(s), returning a table of ordered results.

If an empty "slice" is located, that part will be returned as an empty string. For instance string.split("abc||def", "|") will return a table with three strings: "abc", "", and "def".

local input = "a,b,c"
local values = input:split(",")
print(values[1], values[2], values[3]) --> "a" "b" "c"

Also note that whitespace from the original string will be preserved, for example string.split("abc _ def", "_") will honor the whitespace on both sides of the _ separator. By default, the separator character is , but you can specify an alternative character or series of characters.

Corner Cases

Empty String

local result = string.split("", ",")
print(#result) --> 1
print(result[1]) --> ""

Empty Slices

local result = string.split("foo,,bar", ",")
print(result[1], result[2], result[3]) --> "foo" "" "bar"

local result2 = string.split(",foo", ",")
print(result2[1], result2[2]) --> "" "foo"

local result3 = string.split("foo,", ",")
print(result3[1], result3[2]) --> "foo" ""

local result4 = string.split(",", ",")
print(result4[1], result4[2]) --> "" ""

local result5 = string.split(",,", ",")
print(result5[1], result5[2], result5[3]) --> "" "" ""

Whitespace Preserved

local result = string.split("   whitespace   ", ",")
print(result[1]) --> "   whitespace   "

local result2 = string.split("foo , bar", ",")
print(result2[1], result2[2]) --> "foo " " bar"

Invalid UTF-8

local result = string.split("\xFF", ",")
print(result[1]) --> "\xFF"

local result = string.split("\xFF,\xFE", ",")
print(result[1], result[2]) --> "\xFF" "\xFE"

Unicode

local result = string.split("我很高兴，你呢？", "，")
print(result[1], result[2]) --> "我很高兴" "你呢？"

local result2 = string.split("hello•world", "•")
print(result2[1], result2[2]) --> "hello" "world"
m.s: Splits a string into parts based on the defined separator character(s), returning a table of ordered results.

p.s: The string to split.
The separator character(s) to be used for splitting the string.

kid.simple: Cuts a string into pieces at every separator and gives back a table (list) of the pieces. The separator defaults to a comma.
kid.example:
local parts = string.split("red,green,blue", ",")
print(parts[1], parts[2], parts[3]) -- red green blue
kid.gotcha: Two separators next to each other give an empty piece: "a,,b" splits into "a", "" and "b". Spaces are kept.

m.d:
Returns the substring of s that starts at byte position i and continues until and including byte position j. Both i and j can be negative: -1 refers to the last byte, -2 to the second-to-last, and so on. The default for i is 1 (the beginning) and j defaults to -1 (the end).

If the resolved i is less than 1, it is corrected to 1. If j exceeds the string length, it is corrected to the string length. If after these corrections i is greater than j, the function returns an empty string.

local s = "Hello, world!"
print(string.sub(s, 1, 5))   -- Hello
print(string.sub(s, 8))      -- world!
print(string.sub(s, -6))     -- orld!
print(string.sub(s, -6, -2)) -- orld

-- Extract file extension
local filename = "script.lua"
local dot = string.find(filename, "%.")
print(string.sub(filename, dot + 1)) -- lua

-- Empty result when start > end
print(string.sub("abc", 3, 1)) -- (empty string)
m.s: Returns the substring of `s` that starts at `i` and continues until and including `j`. `i` and `j` can be negative. `i` defaults to `1` and `j` defaults to `-1`.

p.s: The source string to extract a substring from.
The starting byte position of the substring (negative values count from the end).
The ending byte position of the substring, inclusive (negative values count from the end).

kid.simple: Cuts out a piece of a string, from position i to position j (both included). Negative numbers count from the end: -1 is the last character.
kid.example:
local s = "Hello, world!"
print(string.sub(s, 1, 5))  -- Hello
print(string.sub(s, -6))    -- world!
print(string.sub(s, 8, 8))  -- w

m.d: Extracts the values packed in the provided binary string based on the first argument, format, which should match the one originally used to pack() the string; see here for options. The optional third parameter determines the byte at which the reading starts.
m.s: Extracts the values packed in the provided binary string.

p.s: The format string that describes how the binary data was packed.
The binary string to unpack values from.
The byte position in data at which to begin reading.

r.s: The values packed into the provided binary string, plus the index of the first unread byte.

kid.simple: Advanced. Reads values back out of a binary string made by `string.pack`, using the same format code.
kid.example:
local packed = string.pack("i4", 1000)
print(string.unpack("i4", packed)) -- 1000 5 (the value, then the next read position)

m.d:
Returns a copy of the string s with all lowercase ASCII letters (a-z) changed to their uppercase equivalents (A-Z). Characters outside the ASCII letter range, including accented or multibyte characters, are left unchanged.

print(string.upper("hello")) -- HELLO
print(string.upper("Hello World!")) -- HELLO WORLD!

-- Non-letter characters are unaffected
print(string.upper("roblox 123!")) -- ROBLOX 123!

-- Only ASCII letters are converted
print(string.upper("abc ABC")) -- ABC ABC
m.s: Returns a copy of a string with all lowercase letters changed to uppercase.

p.s: The string to convert to uppercase.

kid.simple: Gives back a copy with all a to z letters made UPPERCASE.
kid.example: print(string.upper("hello")) -- HELLO

kid.simple: A string is a piece of text, like "Hello" or a player's name. The string library is a toolbox for working with text: making it UPPERCASE, cutting out a piece, finding a word, replacing words, splitting text into parts, and building text with numbers inside.
kid.analogy: If a string is a strip of paper with letters on it, the string library is your scissors, glue, highlighter and stamp set for that paper.
whenToUse: Show a nice message with numbers, like "Coins: 150" or "Time: 01:05" (`string.format`)
Check a chat command like "/fly" (`string.sub`, `string.lower`, `string.split`)
Find or replace words in text (`string.find`, `string.gsub`)
Pull numbers out of text (`string.match`)
kid.where: A built-in library, so there is nothing to get. Works in any script. You can also call these on a string directly with a colon: `name:upper()` is the same as `string.upper(name)`.

terms.string: Text in your code, written inside quotes, like "Hello" or 'Hi'.
terms.character: One letter, digit, space or symbol in a string. "Hi!" has 3 characters.
terms.index (position): A character's place number, starting at 1. In "Roblox", R is at 1 and x is at 6. Negative numbers count from the end: -1 is the last character.
terms.substring: A smaller piece cut out of a string. "Rob" is a substring of "Roblox".
terms.pattern: A special search code. `%d` means any digit, `%a` any letter, `%s` any space, and `+` means "one or more". So `%d+` finds a whole number like 42.
terms.capture: Parts of a pattern inside parentheses `( )`. Whatever they match is handed back to you separately.
terms.byte: A small number (0 to 255) that the computer uses to store one character. "A" is stored as 65.
terms.ASCII: The basic set of English letters, digits and symbols. Functions like `upper` and `lower` only change the plain A to Z letters.
terms.concatenate: To join strings together. In Luau you use `..`, like "Hello " .. name.
terms.iterator: A function that gives you the next item each time it is called, used in a `for` loop.
terms.binary: Data stored as raw bytes instead of readable text. Used for packing data tightly.

examples.title: Show a nice timer and score
examples.code:
local seconds = 125
local minutes = math.floor(seconds / 60) -- 2
local leftover = seconds % 60            -- 5

-- %02d means: a whole number, at least 2 digits, pad with 0
local timerText = string.format("%02d:%02d", minutes, leftover)
print(timerText) -- 02:05

-- %s puts in any text, %.1f a decimal number with 1 digit after the dot
print(string.format("%s has %d coins and %.1f%% health", "Alex", 150, 87.26))
-- Alex has 150 coins and 87.3% health
explain: `string.format` builds text from a template. Each `%` code is a slot filled by the next value.
`%d` is a whole number, `%02d` a whole number padded to 2 digits, `%s` any text, `%.1f` a decimal rounded to 1 place.
`%%` means a real percent sign.

examples.title: A simple chat command
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    player.Chatted:Connect(function(message)
        -- "/Speed 50" -> {"/Speed", "50"}
        local parts = string.split(message, " ")
        local command = string.lower(parts[1]) -- "/speed"

        if command == "/speed" then
            local amount = tonumber(parts[2]) -- turn "50" into the number 50
            local character = player.Character
            if amount and character then
                character.Humanoid.WalkSpeed = math.clamp(amount, 0, 100)
            end
        end
    end)
end)
explain: `string.split` cuts the message at every space and gives back a table of pieces.
`string.lower` makes the command lowercase so "/SPEED" and "/speed" both work.
`tonumber` turns the text "50" into the number 50 (or nil if it is not a number).

gotchas: Positions start at 1, not 0.
Strings never change in place. `string.upper(name)` gives back a NEW string; `name` itself stays the same. Save the result: `name = name:upper()`.
In `find`, `match`, `gsub` and `gmatch`, some symbols are special pattern codes: `( ) . % + - * ? [ ] ^ $`. To search for a real dot, write `%.`. Or pass `true` for the plain option in `string.find`.
Emojis and accented letters take more than one byte, so `string.len`, `string.sub` and `string.reverse` can split them strangely. Use the `utf8` library for those.
Use a colon to call on a string: `text:upper()`. With a dot you must pass the string yourself: `string.upper(text)`.

library/table.d: This library provides generic functions for table/array manipulation, providing all its functions inside the global table variable. Most functions in the table library assume that the table represents an array or a list. For these functions, the "length" of a table means the result of the length operator.

m.d:
Sets the value for all keys within the given table to nil. This causes the # operator to return 0 for the given table. The allocated capacity of the table's array portion is maintained, which allows for efficient re-use of the space.

local grades = {95, 82, 71, 92, 100, 60}
print(grades[4], #grades) --> 92, 6
table.clear(grades)
print(grades[4], #grades) --> nil, 0
-- If grades is filled again with the same number of entries,
-- no potentially expensive array resizing will occur
-- because the capacity was maintained by table.clear.

This function does not delete/destroy the table provided to it. This function is meant to be used specifically for tables that are to be re-used.
m.s: Sets all keys in the given table to `nil`.

p.s: The table whose keys will be cleared.

kid.simple: Empties a table: every key is set to nil, so `#t` becomes 0. The table itself is kept, so you can refill it quickly.

m.d:
Returns an unfrozen shallow copy of the provided table.

local original = {
    key = "value",
    engine = "Roblox",
    playerID = 505306092
}

local clone = table.clone(original)
m.s: Returns a shallow copy of the provided table.

p.s: The table to be cloned.

r.s: The clone of the provided table.

kid.simple: Makes a copy of a table, so changing the copy does not change the original. It is a shallow copy: tables inside are shared.
kid.example:
local original = {coins = 10}
local copy = table.clone(original)
copy.coins = 99
print(original.coins) -- 10, the original did not change

m.d: Given an array where all elements are strings or numbers, returns the string t[i] ... sep ... t[i+1] ... sep ... t[j]. The default value for sep is an empty string, the default for i is 1, and the default for j is #t. If i is greater than j, returns the empty string.
m.s: Returns the given range of table elements as a string where each element is separated by the given separator.

p.s: The table that will be converted into a string.
The string that will be concatenated between each entry in the table.
The starting index of the table concatenation.
The ending index of the table concatenation.

r.s: The concatenated string of table elements joined by the separator.

kid.simple: Joins a list of strings or numbers into one string, with an optional separator between them. You can also choose a start and end position.
kid.example:
print(table.concat({"a", "b", "c"}, "-")) -- a-b-c
print(table.concat({1, 2, 3}))           -- 123
kid.gotcha: Every item must be a string or number; anything else causes an error.

m.d:
Creates a table with the array portion allocated to the given number of elements, optionally filled with the given value.

local t = table.create(3, "Roblox")
print(table.concat(t)) --> RobloxRobloxRoblox

If you are inserting into large array-like tables and are certain of a reasonable upper limit to the number of elements, it's recommended to use this function to initialize the table. This ensures the table's array portion of its memory is sufficiently sized, as resizing it can be expensive. For small quantities this is typically not noticeable.
m.s: Returns a new table populated with many instances of the specified value.

p.s: The number of elements to allocate in the array portion of the new table.
The value to fill each element with. If omitted, elements are left as nil.

r.s: A new table with the array portion pre-allocated to count elements, filled with value if provided.

kid.simple: Makes a new list with room for a certain number of items, optionally filled with the same value. Good for speed when you know how big a list will be.
kid.example:
local row = table.create(3, 0)
print(table.concat(row, ",")) -- 0,0,0

m.d:
Within the given array-like table haystack, find the first occurrence of value needle, starting from index init or the beginning if not provided. If the value is not found, nil is returned.

A linear search algorithm is performed.

local t = {"a", "b", "c", "d", "e"}
print(table.find(t, "d")) --> 4
print(table.find(t, "z")) --> nil, because z is not in the table
print(table.find(t, "b", 3)) --> nil, because b appears before index 3
m.s: Returns the index of the first occurrence of `needle` within `haystack` starting from `init`.

p.s: The array-like table to search through.
The value to search for within the table.
The index at which to begin searching. Defaults to 1.

r.s: The numeric index of the first occurrence of needle, or nil if not found.

kid.simple: Looks through a list for a value and gives back its position, or nil if it is not there. An optional 3rd number says where to start looking.
kid.gotcha: It only searches number positions (lists), not dictionary keys.

m.d: Iterates over the provided table, passing the key and value of each iteration over to the provided function. This function has been deprecated and is not recommended for use in new code; use a for loop instead.
m.s: Iterates over the provided table, passing the key and value of each iteration over to the provided function.

p.s: The table to be iterated over.
The function that will be used for the iteration. This function will receive 2 arguments for each iteration, where the 1st argument is the key, and the 2nd argument is the value.

kid.simple: Old — use a `for key, value in t do` loop instead.

m.d: This is similar to table.foreach() except that index-value pairs are passed, not key-value pairs. This function has been deprecated and is not recommended for use in new code; use a for loop instead.
m.s: Similar to `Library.table.foreach()` except index-value pairs are passed instead of key-value pairs.

p.s: The table to be iterated over.
The function that will be used for the iteration. This function will receive 2 arguments for each iteration, where the 1st argument is the index, and the 2nd argument is the value.

kid.simple: Old — use a `for i, value in ipairs(t) do` loop instead.

m.d:
This function makes the given table read-only, effectively "freezing" it in its current state. Attempting to modify a frozen table throws an error.

This freezing effect is shallow, which means that you can write to a table within a frozen table. To deep freeze a table, call this function recursively on all of the descending tables.
m.s: Makes the given table read-only.

p.s: The table to be frozen.

r.s: The frozen table.

kid.simple: Locks a table so it can never be changed again. Good for settings that should stay the same. Only the outer table is locked; tables inside it are not.
kid.example:
local SETTINGS = table.freeze({maxPlayers = 10})
-- SETTINGS.maxPlayers = 20  -- this would cause an error
print(SETTINGS.maxPlayers) -- 10

m.d: Returns the number of elements in the table passed. This function has been deprecated and is not recommended for use in new code; use #t instead.
m.s: Returns the number of elements in the table passed.

p.s: The table whose size is being measured.

r.s: The length of the array portion of the table, equivalent to the # operator.

kid.simple: Old — use the `#` operator instead, like `#list`.

m.d:
Inserts value into array t at position pos, shifting up the elements t[pos], t[pos+1], ..., t[#t] by one position. The position must be between 1 and #t (inclusive) for the shift to occur; the value is then written at t[pos].

local t = {"a", "b", "c"}
table.insert(t, 2, "new")
print(table.concat(t, ", ")) --> a, new, b, c
m.s: Inserts the provided value to the target position of the array.

p.s: The table that is being appended to.
The position at which the value will be inserted.
The value that will be appended to the table.

kid.simple: Adds a value to a list. `table.insert(list, value)` puts it at the end. `table.insert(list, position, value)` squeezes it in at that position and slides the rest up by one.

m.d: This function returns true if the given table is frozen and false if it isn't frozen. You can freeze tables using table.freeze().
m.s: Returns `true` if the given table is frozen and `false` if it isn't frozen.

p.s: The table to check.

r.s: Whether the table is frozen from table.freeze().

kid.simple: True if the table has been locked with `table.freeze`.
kid.example:
local t = table.freeze({})
print(table.isfrozen(t)) -- true

m.d: Returns the maximum numeric key of the provided table, or zero if the table has no numeric keys. Gaps in the table are ignored.
m.s: Returns the maximum numeric key of the provided table, or zero if the table has no numeric keys.

p.s: The table to scan for numeric keys.

r.s: The largest positive numeric key in the table, or 0 if the table has no numeric keys.

kid.simple: Gives the biggest number key in a table, even if there are gaps. 0 if there are no number keys.
kid.example:
local t = {[1] = "a", [5] = "b"}
print(table.maxn(t)) -- 5

m.d:
Copies elements in table src from src[a] up to src[b] into table dst starting at index t. Equivalent to the assignment statement dst[t], ..., dst[t + (b - a)] = src[a], ..., src[b].

The default for dst is src. The destination range may overlap with the source range. Returns dst for convenience.

local sourceTable = {4, 5} -- Table of data to copy from
local destTable = {1, 2, 3} -- Table to add copied data to

table.move(
    sourceTable, -- Source table
    1, -- Index to start from in source table
    #sourceTable, -- Index up to (and including) from source table
    #destTable + 1, -- Index within destination table to move data into
    destTable -- Destination table
)
print(destTable) --> {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
m.s: Copies the specified range of elements from one table to another.

p.s: Source table.
Start copying at src[a].
Copy up to and including src[b].
Copy into dst[t], ....
Destination table.

r.s: dst for convenience.

kid.simple: Copies a range of items from one list into a list (the same one or another), starting at a chosen position. Gives back the destination list.

m.d:
Returns a new table with all arguments stored into keys 1, 2, etc. and with a field "n" with the total number of arguments. Note that the resulting table may not be a sequence.

local t = table.pack(1, 2, 3)
print(table.concat(t, ", ")) --> 1, 2, 3
m.s: Returns a new table containing the provided values.

p.s: The values to store sequentially in the new table.

r.s: A new table with arguments at keys 1 through n, plus an n field storing the total argument count.

kid.simple: Puts any number of values into a new list, and also stores how many there were in a field called `n`.
kid.example:
local t = table.pack("a", "b", "c")
print(t.n)    -- 3
print(t[2])   -- b

m.d: Removes from array t the element at position pos, returning the value of the removed element. When pos is an integer between 1 and #t, it shifts down the elements t[pos+1], t[pos+2], ..., t[#t] and erases element t[#t]. If the pos parameter is not provided, pos defaults to the length of the table removing the last element.
m.s: Removes the specified element from the array, shifting later elements down to fill in the empty space if possible.

p.s: The table that is having an element removed.
The index of the element being removed.

r.s: The value of the element that was removed, or nothing if the position is out of bounds.

kid.simple: Takes an item out of a list at a position and gives it back. The items after it slide down to fill the gap. With no position, it removes the last item.
kid.example:
local stack = {"a", "b", "c"}
local last = table.remove(stack)     -- removes "c"
local first = table.remove(stack, 1) -- removes "a"
print(last, first, #stack) -- c a 1

m.d:
Sorts elements of array t in a given order, from t[1] to t[#t]. If comp is given, then it must be a function that receives two elements and returns true when the first element must come before the second in the final order.

The error invalid order function for sorting is thrown if both comp(a, b) and comp(b, a) return true.

If comp is not given, then the standard Luau operator < is used instead.
m.s: Sorts table elements using the provided comparison function or the `<` operator.

p.s: The array to sort in place.

An optional comparison function to be used when comparing elements in the table. This function receives two elements, and should return true if the first element should be sorted before the second in the final order.

kid.simple: Puts a list in order, changing the list itself. By default smallest to biggest (or A to Z). Give a function to choose your own order: it gets two items and returns true if the first should come first.
kid.example:
local nums = {5, 2, 9, 1}
table.sort(nums)
print(table.concat(nums, ",")) -- 1,2,5,9

table.sort(nums, function(a, b) return a > b end)
print(table.concat(nums, ",")) -- 9,5,2,1
kid.gotcha: Your function must be consistent. If it says both a before b AND b before a, you get an "invalid order function" error. Use `>` or `<`, never `>=`.

m.d:
Returns the elements from the given list. By default, i is 1 and j is the length of list.

Note that this same functionality is also provided by the global LuaGlobals.unpack() function.
m.s: Returns all elements from the given list as a tuple.

p.s: The list of elements to be unpacked.
The index of the first element to unpack.
The index of the last element to unpack.

r.s: The elements list[i], list[i+1], ..., list[j] as individual return values.

kid.simple: Takes the items out of a list and gives them back as separate values. Handy to pass a list's items into a function.
kid.example:
local nums = {3, 7, 1}
print(math.max(table.unpack(nums))) -- 7
local a, b = table.unpack({"x", "y"})
print(a, b) -- x y

kid.simple: A table is Luau's way of storing a bunch of values together, like a list of player names or a list of scores. The table library is a toolbox for lists: add items, remove items, find an item, sort the list, join it into text, copy it, and more.
kid.analogy: A table is like a numbered row of lockers. The table library is the school janitor who can add a new locker at the end, take one out and slide the others over, find which locker holds your backpack, or line them up in order.
whenToUse: Keep a list of things and add to it (`table.insert`)
Take things out of a list (`table.remove`)
Check if something is in a list (`table.find`)
Put a leaderboard in order (`table.sort`)
Turn a list into one piece of text (`table.concat`)
kid.where: A built-in library, so there is nothing to get. Works in any script.

terms.table: A container that holds many values. Make one with curly braces: `local fruits = {"apple", "banana"}`.
terms.array (list): A table where items are stored at number positions 1, 2, 3 and so on, in order.
terms.dictionary: A table where items are stored under names (keys) instead of numbers, like `{coins = 10, level = 3}`.
terms.index: The number position of an item in a list. Luau lists start at 1, so `fruits[1]` is the first item.
terms.key / value: In a table, the key is the label (like 1 or "coins") and the value is what is stored there (like "apple" or 10).
terms.length (#): How many items a list has. `#fruits` gives it.
terms.nil: Means "nothing" or "no value". Setting an item to nil removes it.
terms.shallow copy: A copy of the table itself, but any tables INSIDE it are shared with the original, not copied.
terms.frozen: Locked so it cannot be changed. Trying to change a frozen table causes an error.
terms.tuple: Several values handed back at once, like `local a, b, c = table.unpack(list)`.
terms.comparison function: A function you give to `table.sort` that takes two items and returns true if the first should come BEFORE the second.

examples.title: A to-do list: add, remove, find
examples.code:
local tasks = {"Collect coins", "Beat the boss"}

table.insert(tasks, "Find the key")       -- add at the end
table.insert(tasks, 1, "Say hi")          -- add at position 1, others slide up
print(table.concat(tasks, ", "))
-- Say hi, Collect coins, Beat the boss, Find the key

local spot = table.find(tasks, "Beat the boss")
print(spot) -- 3

table.remove(tasks, spot)                 -- take it out, others slide down
print(#tasks) -- 3
print(table.concat(tasks, ", "))
-- Say hi, Collect coins, Find the key
explain: `table.insert(list, value)` adds at the end. With a position first, it squeezes the value in there.
`table.find` tells you where an item is (or nil if it is not there).
`table.remove(list, position)` takes an item out and closes the gap.
`table.concat` joins the list into one string, with ", " between items.

examples.title: Sort a leaderboard from highest to lowest
examples.code:
local scores = {
    {name = "Ava", points = 40},
    {name = "Ben", points = 95},
    {name = "Cal", points = 70},
}

-- return true if a should come before b
table.sort(scores, function(a, b)
    return a.points > b.points -- bigger points first
end)

for place, entry in scores do
    print(place .. ". " .. entry.name .. " - " .. entry.points)
end
-- 1. Ben - 95
-- 2. Cal - 70
-- 3. Ava - 40
explain: Each item is a small table with a name and points.
`table.sort` puts the list in order. Our function says: a goes first if it has MORE points.
Without a function, `table.sort` puts plain numbers or strings from smallest to biggest.

gotchas: Lists start at 1, not 0.
Most table functions only work on lists (number positions 1, 2, 3...). They ignore dictionary keys like `coins`.
Do not use `table.remove` while looping forward through the same list; items slide and you will skip some. Loop backwards instead: `for i = #list, 1, -1 do`.
`#list` can be wrong if the list has holes (a nil in the middle). Use `table.remove` instead of setting items to nil.
`table.clone` only copies the outer table. Tables inside it are still shared.

library/task.d:
The task library allows for functions and threads to be scheduled with the engine's scheduler.

The functions available in this library generally support functions and threads. In most cases using a function is sufficient, but for more advanced cases it's recommended you familiarize yourself with the coroutine library.
library/task.s: Allows for functions and threads to be coordinated with the engine's scheduler.

m.d:
Accepts a function or a thread (as returned by coroutine.create()) and calls/resumes it immediately through the engine's scheduler. Arguments after the first are sent to the function/thread.

If the calling script is currently running in a serial execution phase, then the spawned function or thread is resumed in the current serial execution phase. If the calling script is currently running in a parallel execution phase, then the spawned function or thread is resumed in the current parallel execution phase. For more information, see Parallel Luau.
m.s: Calls/resumes a function/coroutine immediately through the engine's scheduler.

p.s: A function or a thread returned by coroutine.create().
Arguments to send to the function or thread.

r.s: The scheduled thread.

kid.simple: Runs a function (or resumes a thread) RIGHT NOW as its own separate thread. If that function yields (for example with `task.wait`), your code carries on instead of waiting for it. Any extra values you pass go into the function. It gives back the thread it made.
kid.example:
local function greet(name)
    task.wait(2) -- pauses only this greet thread
    print("Hello, " .. name)
end

task.spawn(greet, "Alex") -- starts now; "Alex" is passed to name
print("This prints first, before Hello, Alex")

m.d:
Accepts a function or a thread (as returned by coroutine.create()) and defers it until the end of the current resume point within the current frame.

This function should be used when a similar behavior to task.spawn() is desirable, but the thread does not need to run immediately.

If the calling script is currently running in a serial execution phase, then the deferred function or thread is resumed in a serial execution phase. If the calling script is currently running in a parallel execution phase, then the deferred function or thread is resumed in a parallel execution phase. For more information, see Parallel Luau.
m.s: Calls/resumes a function/coroutine at the end of the current resumption cycle.

p.s: A function or a thread returned by coroutine.create.
Arguments to send to the function or thread.

r.s: The scheduled thread.

kid.simple: Like `task.spawn`, but it does not run immediately. It waits until the code that is running right now reaches its next pause point (finishes or yields), and then runs, still in the same frame. Use it when something should happen "right after this".
kid.example:
task.defer(function()
    print("2: deferred")
end)
print("1: this finishes first")

m.d:
Accepts a function or a thread (as returned by coroutine.create()) and schedules it to be called/resumed on the next Heartbeat after the given amount of time in seconds has elapsed. Arguments after the second are sent to the function/thread.

This function differs from the deprecated global delay() function in that no throttling occurs: on the very same Heartbeat step in which enough time has passed, the function is guaranteed to be called/resumed. Providing a duration of zero (0) will guarantee that the function is called on the very next Heartbeat.

You can calculate the actual time passed by calling os.clock() upon scheduling and in the scheduled function.

If the calling script is currently running in a serial execution phase, then the delayed function or thread is resumed in a serial execution phase. If the calling script is currently running in a parallel execution phase, then the delayed function or thread is resumed in a parallel execution phase. For more information, see Parallel Luau.
m.s: Schedules a function/coroutine to be called/resumed on the next Heartbeat after the given duration (in seconds) has passed, without throttling.

p.s: The minimum number of seconds that must pass before the function/thread is called/resumed.
A function or a thread returned by coroutine.create() to be called/resumed after the duration elapses.
Arguments to be passed to the function/thread when it is due to be called/resumed.

r.s: The scheduled thread.

kid.simple: Schedules a function to run after a number of seconds, without pausing your code now. Extra values after the function are passed into it. It gives back a thread, which you can stop with `task.cancel`.
kid.example:
local part = workspace:WaitForChild("Bomb")

task.delay(3, function()
    part:Destroy() -- after 3 seconds, the bomb disappears
end)
print("The countdown has started") -- runs right away
kid.gotcha: `task.delay(0, f)` runs `f` on the very next frame (next Heartbeat), not instantly.

m.d:
If the calling script is currently running in a serial execution phase, desynchronize() suspends the script and the script will be resumed in the next parallel execution phase. If the calling script is currently running in a parallel execution phase, desynchronize() returns immediately and has no effect.

Only scripts which are descendants of an Actor may call this method. If a script outside of an Actor calls this method, an error will be raised. ModuleScripts may also call desynchronize() as long as the instantiation of the module calling it was required by a script that is a descendant of an Actor.

For more information, see Parallel Luau.
m.s: Causes the following code to be run in parallel.

kid.simple: Advanced (Parallel Luau). Switches the script into parallel mode so it can run at the same time as other scripts on other processor cores. Only works for scripts inside an `Actor`; otherwise it errors. If you are already in parallel mode, it does nothing.
kid.example:
-- Script inside an Actor (advanced)
task.desynchronize()
-- heavy math here can run in parallel with other Actors
local total = 0
for i = 1, 1000000 do total += i end
task.synchronize() -- go back before changing parts in Workspace
kid.gotcha: In parallel mode you cannot change most things in the game world. Call `task.synchronize()` first.

m.d:
If the calling script is currently running in a parallel execution phase, synchronize() suspends the script and the script will be resumed in the next serial execution phase. If the calling script is currently running in a serial execution phase, synchronize() returns immediately and has no effect.

Only scripts which are descendants of an Actor may call this method. If a script outside of an Actor calls this method, an error will be raised. ModuleScripts may also call synchronize() as long as the instantiation of the module calling it was required by a script that is a descendant of an Actor.

For more information, see Parallel Luau.
m.s: Causes the following code to be run in serial.

kid.simple: Advanced (Parallel Luau). Switches the script back to normal one-at-a-time (serial) mode, where it is safe to change the game world. Only for scripts inside an `Actor`. If you are already in serial mode, it does nothing.
kid.example:
-- Script inside an Actor (advanced)
task.desynchronize()
local result = 2 + 2 -- parallel-safe work
task.synchronize()
workspace.Part.Name = tostring(result) -- safe to change the world now

m.d:
Yields the current thread until the given duration (in seconds) has elapsed, then resumes the thread on the next Heartbeat step. The actual amount of time elapsed is returned.

If no duration is given, it will default to zero (0). This means the thread resumes on the very next step, which is equivalent in behavior to RunService.Heartbeat:Wait()

Unlike the deprecated global wait(), this function does not throttle and guarantees the resumption of the thread on the first Heartbeat that occurs when it is due. This function also only returns the elapsed time and nothing else.

If the calling script is currently running in a serial execution phase, then the script is resumed in a serial execution phase. If the calling script is currently running in a parallel execution phase, then the script is resumed in a parallel execution phase. For more information, see Parallel Luau.
m.s: Yields the current thread without throttling.

p.s: The amount of time in seconds that should elapse before the current thread is resumed.

kid.simple: Pauses (yields) the current script for the number of seconds you give, then continues on the next frame after that time has passed. It returns how many seconds really passed. With no number, it waits just one frame.
kid.example:
print("Waiting...")
local actual = task.wait(2) -- pause this script for about 2 seconds
print("Waited", actual, "seconds") -- e.g. 2.008

task.wait() -- wait just one frame (about 0.016 seconds)
kid.gotcha: It never waits LESS than you asked, but it can be a little more because it wakes on the next frame.

m.d:
Cancels a thread and closes it, preventing it from being resumed manually or by the engine's scheduler.

This function can be used with other members of the task library that return a thread to cancel them before they are resumed. For example:

local thread = task.delay(5, function()
    print("Hello world!")
end)

task.cancel(thread)

Note that threads may be in a state where it is impossible to cancel them. For example, the currently executing thread and threads that have resumed another coroutine may not be cancelled. If this is the case, an error will be generated. However, code should not rely on specific thread states or conditions causing task.cancel() to fail. It is possible that future updates will eliminate these constraints and allow threads in these states to be successfully cancelled.
m.s: Cancels a thread, preventing it from being resumed.

p.s: The thread that will be cancelled.

kid.simple: Stops a thread so it never runs (or never continues). Use it with the thread you got back from `task.delay`, `task.spawn` or `task.defer` when you change your mind.
kid.example:
local thread = task.delay(5, function()
    print("You will never see this")
end)

task.cancel(thread) -- cancelled before the 5 seconds were up
kid.gotcha: You cannot cancel the thread that is calling `task.cancel` (the one running right now); that causes an error.

kid.simple: The task library controls WHEN code runs. `task.wait` pauses your script for some seconds. `task.spawn`, `task.defer` and `task.delay` start a function running on the side, so your main code keeps going without waiting for it. `task.cancel` stops something you scheduled.
kid.analogy: Think of a kitchen. `task.wait(5)` is you standing by the oven for 5 minutes. `task.spawn` is handing a job to a helper right now while you keep cooking. `task.defer` is a sticky note saying "helper, do this as soon as I finish what I am doing right now". `task.delay(5, ...)` is setting a kitchen timer that tells the helper to start in 5 minutes. `task.cancel` is tearing up the note before the helper starts.
whenToUse: Pause between steps, like a countdown: `task.wait(1)`
Run a loop forever without freezing the rest of your script: `task.spawn`
Do something later without stopping now, like removing a power-up after 10 seconds: `task.delay`
Let the current code finish first, then run something: `task.defer`
Stop a scheduled job that is no longer needed: `task.cancel`
kid.where: A built-in library, so there is nothing to get. Use `task.wait`, `task.spawn` and friends in any Script, LocalScript or ModuleScript, on the server or the client.

terms.yield: To pause. When code yields, it stops at that line and lets the rest of the game keep running, then continues later from the same line. `task.wait` yields.
terms.thread: One line of work that the game is doing. Your script is a thread. `task.spawn` makes a new thread that runs alongside yours, like a second worker.
terms.scheduler: The part of the engine that decides which thread runs next and when to wake up paused ones.
terms.frame: One picture the game draws, about 60 per second. Each frame, the game also wakes up threads that are done waiting.
terms.Heartbeat: The moment at the end of every frame when waiting threads wake up. See RunService.Heartbeat.
terms.coroutine: A function that can pause in the middle and be continued later. `task` functions can take one (a thread) instead of a plain function.
terms.throttle: To slow things down on purpose. The old `wait()` did this when the game was busy; `task.wait` does not.
terms.parallel / serial: Serial means one thing at a time, in order. Parallel means many things truly at the same time on different processor cores. Parallel Luau is an advanced feature that needs an `Actor` object.
terms.Actor: A special container object. Scripts inside an Actor can run some code in parallel.

examples.title: Yielding: wait pauses YOUR script
examples.code:
print("3")
task.wait(1) -- this script pauses here for about 1 second
print("2")
task.wait(1)
print("1")
task.wait(1)
print("Go!")
explain: `task.wait(1)` yields: this script stops at that line for about 1 second.
While it waits, the rest of the game (other scripts, physics, players) keeps running normally.
After the time is up, the script continues on the next line.

examples.title: spawn vs defer vs delay: who prints first?
examples.code:
print("A: start")

task.delay(2, function()
    print("E: delay - runs about 2 seconds later")
end)

task.defer(function()
    print("D: defer - runs after the current code is finished")
end)

task.spawn(function()
    print("B: spawn - runs right away")
    task.wait(1) -- only pauses THIS spawned function, not the main script
    print("F (after 1 second): spawn continues")
end)

print("C: main script keeps going, it did not wait")
explain: The output order is A, B, C, D, then F after 1 second, then E after 2 seconds.
`task.spawn` runs its function immediately, until that function yields (here, `task.wait(1)`). Then the main script continues.
`task.defer` waits politely: it runs once the current bit of code (the rest of this script) is done, still in the same frame.
`task.delay(2, ...)` runs the function after 2 seconds, and the main script does not wait for it.
The `task.wait(1)` inside the spawned function only pauses that function. The main script is a different thread and is not paused.

examples.title: A loop that runs forever without blocking the rest
examples.code:
local part = workspace:WaitForChild("Lamp")

-- this loop never ends, so we run it in its own thread
task.spawn(function()
    while true do
        part.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0) -- red
        task.wait(0.5)
        part.Color = Color3.fromRGB(0, 0, 255) -- blue
        task.wait(0.5)
    end
end)

-- without task.spawn, this line would never run
print("Lamp is flashing, and I can keep doing other things")
explain: A `while true do` loop never finishes. If it was in the main script, any code after it would never run.
Putting it inside `task.spawn` gives it its own thread, so the print below still runs.
Every loop that runs forever MUST have a `task.wait` inside, or the game freezes.

examples.title: A speed boost that ends after 5 seconds, and can be cancelled
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    player.CharacterAdded:Connect(function(character)
        local humanoid = character:WaitForChild("Humanoid")
        humanoid.WalkSpeed = 32 -- boost!

        -- schedule the boost to end in 5 seconds, without pausing this function
        local resetThread = task.delay(5, function()
            humanoid.WalkSpeed = 16 -- back to normal
        end)

        -- if the player dies first, cancel the scheduled reset
        humanoid.Died:Connect(function()
            task.cancel(resetThread)
        end)
    end)
end)
explain: When a character spawns, we double their walking speed.
`task.delay` sets up the reset for 5 seconds later and gives back the thread it made.
If the player dies before then, `task.cancel` throws away the reset so it never runs.

gotchas: Use `task.wait`, not the old `wait`. The old one can wait longer than asked when the game is busy.
A `while true do` loop with no `task.wait` inside freezes the game (and Studio). Always wait inside endless loops.
`task.wait` only pauses the script (thread) it is in. It does not pause other scripts or a function you started with `task.spawn`.
`task.wait(0.1)` waits AT LEAST 0.1 seconds. It wakes on the next frame after the time is up, so it may be a tiny bit longer. It returns the real time that passed.
Code inside `task.spawn` or `task.delay` runs separately. If it errors, your main script keeps going, but the spawned function stops.
Do not forget the comma: `task.delay(3, myFunction)`, and pass the function itself (`myFunction`), not the result of calling it (`myFunction()`).

library/utf8.d:
This library provides basic support for UTF-8 encoding. This library does not provide any support for Unicode other than the handling of the encoding. Any operation that needs the meaning of a character, such as character classification, is outside its scope.

Unless stated otherwise, all functions that expect a byte position as a parameter assume that the given position is either the start of a byte sequence or one plus the length of the subject string. As in the string library, negative indices count from the end of the string.

You can find a large catalog of usable UTF-8 characters here.
library/utf8.s: This library provides basic support for `UTF-8` encoding.

m.d: The pattern "[%z\x01-\x7F\xC2-\xF4][\x80-\xBF]*", which matches exactly zero or more UTF-8 byte sequence, assuming that the subject is a valid UTF-8 string.
m.s: The pattern `"[%z\x01-\x7F\xC2-\xF4][\x80-\xBF]*"`, which matches exactly zero or more UTF-8 byte sequences, assuming that the subject is a valid UTF-8 string.

local str = "héllo"

If the specified character is neither in the subject nor right after its end, the function returns nil.

Returns an iterator function so that

for first, last in utf8.graphemes(str) do
