library/vector.d:
This library implements functionality for the vector type in addition to the built-in primitive operator support. It uses vectors with three components (x, y, and z).

Individual vector components can be accessed using the fields x or X, y or Y, z or Z. Since vector values are immutable, writing to individual components is not supported.

m.d: A pre-allocated constant equivalent to vector.create(0, 0, 0). Useful as a default value or additive identity in vector arithmetic without allocating a new vector each time.
m.s: Constant vector with all components set to `0`.

kid.simple: A ready-made vector of (0, 0, 0).
kid.example: print(vector.zero) --> 0, 0, 0

m.d: A pre-allocated constant equivalent to vector.create(1, 1, 1). Useful as a multiplicative identity or scale factor in vector arithmetic without allocating a new vector each time.
m.s: Constant vector with all components set to `1`.

kid.simple: A ready-made vector of (1, 1, 1). Multiply it to get an even size.
kid.example: print(vector.one * 4) --> 4, 4, 4

m.d: Creates a new vector with the given component values. The z parameter defaults to 0 when omitted, so vector.create(1, 2) is equivalent to vector.create(1, 2, 0).
m.s: Creates a new vector with the given component values.

p.s: The x component of the new vector.
The y component of the new vector.
The z component of the new vector. Defaults to 0 when omitted.

r.s: A new vector with the specified x, y, and z component values.

kid.simple: Makes a new vector from x, y and z. If you leave out z it becomes 0.
kid.example:
local v = vector.create(1, 2, 3)
print(v.x, v.y, v.z) --> 1 2 3
print(vector.create(5, 6)) --> 5, 6, 0

m.d: Returns the magnitude (Euclidean length) of the vector, computed as math.sqrt(vec.x^2 + vec.y^2 + vec.z^2).
m.s: Calculates the magnitude of a given vector.

p.s: The vector whose magnitude is computed.

r.s: The Euclidean length of the vector.

kid.simple: The length of a vector. Use it on the difference of two positions to get the distance between them.
kid.example:
print(vector.magnitude(vector.create(3, 4, 0))) --> 5
local distance = vector.magnitude(vector.create(6, 0, 8) - vector.zero) --> 10

m.d: Returns a unit vector (magnitude of 1) pointing in the same direction as the input. Computed as vec / vector.magnitude(vec). If the input vector has zero magnitude, the result contains nan components.
m.s: Computes the normalized version (unit vector) of a given vector.

p.s: The vector to normalize.

r.s: A unit vector pointing in the same direction as the input.

kid.simple: Makes a copy with length exactly 1 that points the same way (a unit vector). Use it when you only care about direction.
kid.example: print(vector.normalize(vector.create(3, 4, 0))) --> 0.6, 0.8, 0
kid.gotcha: The zero vector has no direction, so normalizing it gives NaN.

m.d: Returns the cross product of two vectors, which is a vector perpendicular to both inputs whose magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram they span. The result is computed as vector.create(vec1.y*vec2.z - vec1.z*vec2.y, vec1.z*vec2.x - vec1.x*vec2.z, vec1.x*vec2.y - vec1.y*vec2.x).
m.s: Computes the cross product of two vectors.

p.s: The first operand vector.
The second operand vector.

r.s: A vector perpendicular to both inputs whose magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram they span.

kid.simple: Gives a new arrow at a right angle (90 degrees) to both arrows. Swapping the order flips it to point the other way.
kid.example:
local right = vector.create(1, 0, 0)
local up = vector.create(0, 1, 0)
print(vector.cross(right, up)) --> 0, 0, 1
print(vector.cross(up, right)) --> 0, 0, -1

m.d: Returns the dot product (scalar product) of two vectors, computed as vec1.x*vec2.x + vec1.y*vec2.y + vec1.z*vec2.z. The result is a single number equal to the product of the magnitudes of the two vectors times the cosine of the angle between them.
m.s: Computes the dot product of two vectors.

p.s: The first operand vector.
The second operand vector.

r.s: The scalar dot product of the two vectors.

kid.simple: One number telling how much two arrows point the same way: multiply matching numbers and add them up. With 1-long arrows: 1 = same way, 0 = right angle, -1 = opposite.
kid.example:
print(vector.dot(vector.create(1, 2, 3), vector.create(4, 5, 6))) --> 32 (1*4 + 2*5 + 3*6)
print(vector.dot(vector.create(1, 0, 0), vector.create(0, 1, 0))) --> 0  (right angle)

m.d: Computes the angle between two vectors in radians. The axis, if specified, is used to determine the sign of the angle.
m.s: Computes the angle between two vectors in radians.

p.s: The first vector.
The second vector.
An optional reference axis used to determine the sign of the returned angle.

r.s: The angle between the two vectors in radians, signed if an axis is provided.

kid.simple: The angle between two vectors, in radians. If you also give an `axis`, the answer gets a plus or minus sign showing which way around it turns.
kid.example:
local a = vector.create(1, 0, 0)
local b = vector.create(0, 1, 0)
print(math.deg(vector.angle(a, b))) --> 90

m.d: Returns a new vector with each component rounded down to the nearest integer, equivalent to vector.create(math.floor(vec.x), math.floor(vec.y), math.floor(vec.z)).
m.s: Applies `Library.math.floor()` to every component of the input vector.

p.s: The vector whose components are rounded down.

r.s: A new vector with each component rounded down to the nearest integer.

kid.simple: Rounds every number DOWN to a whole number.
kid.example: print(vector.floor(vector.create(-2.6, 5.1, 8.8))) --> -3, 5, 8

m.d: Returns a new vector with each component rounded up to the nearest integer, equivalent to vector.create(math.ceil(vec.x), math.ceil(vec.y), math.ceil(vec.z)).
m.s: Applies `Library.math.ceil()` to every component of the input vector.

p.s: The vector whose components are rounded up.

r.s: A new vector with each component rounded up to the nearest integer.

kid.simple: Rounds every number UP to a whole number.
kid.example: print(vector.ceil(vector.create(-2.6, 5.1, 8.8))) --> -2, 6, 9

m.d: Returns a new vector with each component replaced by its absolute value, equivalent to vector.create(math.abs(vec.x), math.abs(vec.y), math.abs(vec.z)).
m.s: Applies `Library.math.abs()` to every component of the input vector.

p.s: The vector whose components are made absolute.

r.s: A new vector with each component replaced by its absolute value.

kid.simple: Removes the minus sign from every number.
kid.example: print(vector.abs(vector.create(-2, 4, -6))) --> 2, 4, 6

m.d: Returns a new vector where each component is 1 if the corresponding input component is positive, -1 if negative, or 0 if zero. Equivalent to vector.create(math.sign(vec.x), math.sign(vec.y), math.sign(vec.z)). The behavior for negative zero and nan is consistent with math.sign.
m.s: Applies `Library.math.sign()` to every component of the input vector.

p.s: The vector whose component signs are extracted.

r.s: A new vector where each component is the sign of the corresponding input component.

kid.simple: Turns each number into -1 (negative), 0 (zero) or 1 (positive).
kid.example: print(vector.sign(vector.create(-2.6, 5.1, 0))) --> -1, 1, 0

m.d: Returns a new vector with each component clamped between the corresponding components of min and max. Each component of max must be greater than or equal to the corresponding component of min; otherwise, an error is raised.
m.s: Applies `Library.math.clamp()` to every component of the input vector.

p.s: The vector whose components are clamped.
The vector of per-component minimum bounds.
The vector of per-component maximum bounds. Each component must be greater than or equal to the corresponding component of min.

r.s: A new vector with each component clamped between the corresponding components of min and max.

kid.simple: Keeps each number between the matching numbers of `min` and `max`, like keeping something inside a box.
kid.example:
local v = vector.create(30, -5, 10)
print(vector.clamp(v, vector.create(-20, 0, -20), vector.create(20, 50, 20))) --> 20, 0, 10
kid.gotcha: Each number in `max` must be greater than or equal to the matching number in `min`, or it errors.

m.d: Returns a vector linearly interpolated between two vectors (vec1, vec2) by the fraction alpha. Note that alpha is not limited to the range [0, 1].
m.s: Returns a vector linearly interpolated between two vectors by a fractional alpha.

p.s: The starting vector (returned when alpha is 0).
The ending vector (returned when alpha is 1).
The interpolation fraction. Not clamped to [0, 1].

r.s: A vector interpolated component-wise between vec1 and vec2.

kid.simple: Finds a point part-way from `vec1` to `vec2`. `alpha` 0 gives vec1, 1 gives vec2, 0.5 gives halfway.
kid.example:
local a = vector.create(0, 0, 0)
local b = vector.create(10, 20, 0)
print(vector.lerp(a, b, 0.5)) --> 5, 10, 0
kid.gotcha: `alpha` is not limited to 0 to 1; numbers outside go past the ends.

m.d: Returns a new vector where each component is the maximum of the corresponding components across all input vectors. Accepts a variadic number of vectors (at least one). When a component is nan in one vector but a valid number in another, the valid number is used.
m.s: Applies `Library.math.max()` to the corresponding components of the input vectors.

p.s: One or more vectors to compare component-wise.

r.s: A new vector where each component is the maximum of the corresponding components across all inputs.

kid.simple: Builds a vector from the BIGGEST x, the biggest y and the biggest z among all the vectors you pass in.
kid.example: print(vector.max(vector.create(1, 5, 2), vector.create(4, 1, 3))) --> 4, 5, 3

m.d: Returns a new vector where each component is the minimum of the corresponding components across all input vectors. Accepts a variadic number of vectors (at least one). When a component is nan in one vector but a valid number in another, the valid number is used.
m.s: Applies `Library.math.min()` to the corresponding components of the input vectors.

p.s: One or more vectors to compare component-wise.

r.s: A new vector where each component is the minimum of the corresponding components across all inputs.

kid.simple: Builds a vector from the SMALLEST x, the smallest y and the smallest z among all the vectors you pass in.
kid.example: print(vector.min(vector.create(1, 5, 2), vector.create(4, 1, 3))) --> 1, 1, 2

kid.simple: `vector` is a toolbox of functions for 3D vectors: groups of three numbers X, Y, Z. It does the same jobs as Vector3's own methods (length, direction, dot, cross, rounding and more), but you call them like `vector.magnitude(v)` instead of `v.Magnitude`. You can use these functions on normal Vector3 values like `part.Position`.
kid.analogy: If a Vector3 is a backpack with its own built-in tools, the `vector` library is a shared tool bench. You bring the backpack to the bench: `vector.magnitude(v)` instead of `v.Magnitude`.
whenToUse: Doing vector math with a function style: `vector.magnitude(a - b)` for distance.
Clamping each number of a position into a box with `vector.clamp`.
Any time you would use Vector3 methods; pick whichever style you like.
kid.where: A built-in Luau library that works in every Script, LocalScript and ModuleScript. Type `vector.` and the function name. No game:GetService needed.

terms.vector: Three numbers (X, Y, Z) that can mean a spot in the world or an arrow with a direction and length.
terms.component: One of the numbers inside a vector: x, y or z.
terms.magnitude: The length of the vector. For a difference of two positions, the distance between them.
terms.normalize: Change a vector's length to exactly 1 but keep its direction. The result is called a unit vector.
terms.unit vector: An arrow exactly 1 long; it only says which way.
terms.dot product: One number showing how much two arrows point the same way: positive = same-ish, 0 = right angle, negative = opposite-ish.
terms.cross product: A new arrow at a right angle (90 degrees) to both input arrows.
terms.radians: The angle unit Roblox math uses. 180 degrees is pi (about 3.1416). Use `math.deg` for degrees.
terms.lerp / interpolate: Find a point part-way between two vectors. 0.5 means halfway.
terms.clamp: Squash each number so it stays between a minimum and a maximum.
terms.immutable: Cannot be changed after it is made. You cannot do `v.x = 5`; make a new vector instead.
terms.NaN: Not a Number: a broken value, for example from normalizing a zero-length vector.

examples.title: Distance and direction with the vector library
examples.place: Script in ServerScriptService (needs Parts named A and B in Workspace)
examples.code:
local a = workspace:WaitForChild("A")
local b = workspace:WaitForChild("B")

local difference = b.Position - a.Position
local distance = vector.magnitude(difference)   -- same as difference.Magnitude
local direction = vector.normalize(difference)  -- same as difference.Unit

print("B is", distance, "studs from A")
print("Direction from A to B:", direction)
explain: `b.Position - a.Position` is the arrow from A to B.
`vector.magnitude` measures its length: the distance.
`vector.normalize` shrinks it to length 1 so it only tells you the direction.

examples.title: Keep a part inside an invisible box
examples.place: Script inside an unanchored Part in Workspace
examples.code:
local part = script.Parent
local boxMin = vector.create(-20, 0, -20)
local boxMax = vector.create(20, 50, 20)

while true do
	local pos = part.Position
	local safe = vector.clamp(pos, boxMin, boxMax)
	if safe ~= pos then
		part.Position = safe -- push it back inside
	end
	task.wait(0.1)
end
explain: `vector.clamp` keeps X between -20 and 20, Y between 0 and 50, and Z between -20 and 20.
If the part wanders outside, it gets placed back on the edge of the box.

gotchas: Vectors cannot be changed piece by piece: `v.x = 5` does not work. Make a new one with `vector.create`.
`vector.normalize` on (0, 0, 0) gives NaN. Check the magnitude first.
`vector.angle` returns radians. Use `math.deg` to see degrees.
In `vector.clamp`, each number of `max` must be at least as big as the matching number of `min`, or it errors.
`vector.create(1, 2)` gives (1, 2, 0): a missing z becomes 0.

global/LuaGlobals.d: The following is a list of functions and variables that are native to Luau. These functions can be used in a standard installation of both Luau and Lua 5.1.4, though there are some differences in how some of these work on Roblox.
global/LuaGlobals.s: A list of functions and variables that are native to Luau.

m.d:
A table that is shared between all scripts of the same context level. Any value written to _G from one script is visible to every other script at that same context level, which makes it a simple way to share state between scripts.

-- Script A (sets a value)
_G.mySharedValue = "hello from Script A"

Note that relying on `_G` for cross-script communication introduces
ordering dependencies and makes code harder to reason about. Prefer
ModuleScript for shared state when possible.
m.s: A table that is shared between all scripts of the same context level.

kid.simple: A shared table every script on the same side (all server Scripts, or all of one player's LocalScripts) can read and write. A quick way to share values, but a ModuleScript is usually cleaner.
kid.example:
-- Script A in ServerScriptService
_G.gameMode = "Hard"

-- Script B in ServerScriptService (runs later)
task.wait(1)
print(_G.gameMode) --> Hard
kid.gotcha: Server `_G` and client `_G` are separate. It also depends on which script runs first. Prefer ModuleScripts.

m.d: A global variable (not a function) that holds a string containing the current interpreter version.
m.s: A global variable that holds a string containing the current interpreter version.

kid.simple: A text value (not a function) that says which language version is running. In Roblox it prints something like `Luau`.
kid.example:
-- Any script
print(_VERSION) --> Luau

m.d: Throws an error if the provided value is false or nil. If the assertion passes, it returns all values passed to it.
m.s: Throws an error if the provided `value` resolves to `false` or `nil`.

p.s: The value that will be asserted against.
The text that will be shown in the error if the assertion fails.

r.s: All values originally passed to assert if the assertion succeeds.

kid.simple: Checks that something is true. If it is false or nil, it stops the script with an error message you choose. Great for catching mistakes early.
kid.example:
-- Any script
local part = workspace:FindFirstChild("Door")
assert(part, "Could not find the Door part!") -- errors if part is nil
print("Found the door")

m.d: Performs the specified operation of the garbage collector. Note that Roblox's Luau sandbox only allows the count option to be used (the total memory in use by Luau, in kilobytes), as other options can interfere with existing processes. Effectively, this makes LuaGlobals.gcinfo() a superior alternative that should be used instead.
m.s: Performs the specified operation of the garbage collector.

p.s: The name of the operation that should be performed by the garbage collector.

r.s: The result of the garbage collector operation; for the count option, returns the total memory in use in kilobytes.

kid.simple: Old — it only works with "count" in Roblox; use gcinfo() to see memory use instead.

m.d:
Terminates the last protected function called and outputs message as an error message. If the function containing the error is not called in a protected function such as pcall(), then the script which called the function will terminate. The error function itself never returns and acts like a script error.

The level argument specifies how to get the error position. With level 1 (the default), the error position is where the error function was called. Level 2 points the error to where the function that called error was called; and so on. Passing a level 0 avoids the addition of error position information to the message.
m.s: Halts thread execution and throws an error.

p.s: The error message to display.
The level of information that should be printed. Defaults to 1.

kid.simple: Stops the current code on purpose and shows an error message. Often used with `pcall` to report problems.
kid.example:
-- Any script
local function setSpeed(speed)
	if type(speed) ~= "number" then
		error("speed must be a number!")
	end
	print("Speed set to", speed)
end

local ok, err = pcall(setSpeed, "fast")
print(ok, err) --> false  ...speed must be a number!

m.d: Returns the total memory heap size in kilobytes. The number reflects the current heap consumption from the operating system perspective, which fluctuates over time as garbage collector frees objects.
m.s: Returns the total memory heap size in kilobytes.

r.s: The total memory heap size in kilobytes.

kid.simple: Tells you how much memory your scripts are using right now, in kilobytes (KB). Useful for spotting leaks while testing.
kid.example:
-- Any script
print("Lua memory used: " .. gcinfo() .. " KB")

m.d:
Returns the current environment in use by the caller, as a dictionary.

  • If provided with a function, the environment of the function will be returned.
  • If provided with an integer, LuaGlobals.getfenv() will provide the environment of the function at the provided stack level: Level 1 is the function calling LuaGlobals.getfenv(). If stack is 0, LuaGlobals.getfenv() returns the global environment of the current script. When using LuaGlobals.getfenv() to get the current environment of a script, it will return the same table every time within the specific thread.

WARNING: This function allows uncontrolled change of the global/function environment and disables script optimizations. Changes to the environment are not tracked by the script analysis tooling and may result in missing or incorrect warnings. As a replacement, consider using debug.info() instead.
m.s: Returns the current environment in use by the caller, as a dictionary.

p.s: The stack level (int) of the environment to be returned; or the function whose environment will be returned.

r.s: The environment table of the specified function or stack level.

m.dep: This function allows uncontrolled change of the global/function environment and disables script optimizations. Changes to the environment are not tracked by the script analysis tooling and may result in missing or incorrect warnings. As a replacement, consider using debug.info() instead.

kid.simple: Old — don't use it; it slows scripts down. Use ModuleScripts and local variables instead.

m.d:
Returns the metatable of the given value t if it has one, otherwise returns nil. If t does have a metatable, and the __metatable metamethod is set, it returns that value instead.

t can be a value of any type, not only a table, and this function doesn't error when t isn't a table. However, it doesn't always return nil for non-table values. Strings and many Roblox types, such as Instance, have locked metatables, so this function returns the string "The metatable is locked" for them. To check whether a value uses a specific metatable, compare the result directly, such as getmetatable(value) == MyClass.
m.s: Returns the metatable of the given value.

p.s: The value to fetch the metatable of.

r.s: The metatable of t, the value of the __metatable metamethod if set, or nil if no metatable exists.

kid.simple: Gets the metatable (secret helper table) of a table, if it has one. Advanced; used when building your own object types.
kid.example:
-- Any script
local helper = { __index = { greet = function() return "hi" end } }
local obj = setmetatable({}, helper)
print(getmetatable(obj) == helper) --> true

m.d: Returns three values: an iterator function, the table t and the number 0. Each time the iterator function is called, it returns the next numerical index-value pair in the table. When used in a generic for-loop, the return values can be used to iterate over each numerical index in the table:
m.s: Returns an iterator function and the table for use in a for loop.

p.s: A table whose elements are to be iterated over.

r.s: An iterator function that returns the next index-value pair on each call.
The table t passed as the invariant state.
The initial control value 0.

kid.simple: Used in a `for` loop to go through a list in order: item 1, item 2, item 3... It stops at the first gap (nil).
kid.example:
-- Any script
local players = { "Ava", "Ben", "Cy" }
for index, name in ipairs(players) do
	print(index, name) --> 1 Ava, 2 Ben, 3 Cy
end

m.d:
Loads Luau code from a string and returns it as a function.

Unlike standard Lua 5.1, Roblox's Luau cannot load the compiled bytecode using loadstring().

loadstring() is disabled by default. For guidance around enabling it, see ServerScriptService.

WARNING: This method disables certain Luau optimizations on the returned function. Extreme caution should be taken when using LuaGlobals.loadstring(); if your intention is to allow users to run code in your experience, make sure to protect the returned function's environment by using LuaGlobals.getfenv() and LuaGlobals.setfenv().
m.s: Returns the provided code as a function that can be executed.

p.s: The specified string to be loaded as Luau code.
An optional chunk name for error messages and debug information. If unspecified, Luau uses the contents string.

r.s: The compiled function on success, or nil followed by an error message string on failure.

kid.simple: Turns text containing Luau code into a function you can run. It is turned off by default for safety, and only the server can turn it on.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService (only if LoadStringEnabled is on)
local fn = loadstring("return 2 + 3")
if fn then
	print(fn()) --> 5
end
kid.gotcha: Running code from players is very dangerous. Almost every game should leave this off.

m.d:
Creates a blank zero-size userdata with the option for it to have a metatable. If addMetatable is true, an empty metatable is created and assigned to the userdata; you can then retrieve it with LuaGlobals.getmetatable() and populate it with metamethods. If addMetatable is false or omitted, the userdata has no metatable and only serves as a unique identity token.

Unlike host-created userdata (Roblox instances), a newproxy-created userdata always reports "userdata" from both LuaGlobals.type() and typeof(); setting a __type metamethod on it does not change the typeof() result.

-- Create a proxy with a metatable to implement custom tostring
local proxy = newproxy(true)
local mt = getmetatable(proxy)

mt.__tostring = function()
    return "MyProxy"
end

print(tostring(proxy)) --> MyProxy
print(type(proxy)) --> userdata
m.s: Creates a blank `userdata`, with the option for it to have a metatable.

p.s: Whether to attach an empty metatable to the new userdata.

r.s: A new blank userdata, with an empty metatable attached if addMetatable is true.

kid.simple: Makes a blank special object (userdata). Advanced; sometimes used as a unique marker or with a metatable for custom behavior.
kid.example:
-- Any script
local marker = newproxy()
print(type(marker)) --> userdata

m.d:
Returns the first key/value pair in the array. If a lastKey argument was specified then returns the next element in the array based on the key that provided. The order in which the indices are enumerated is not specified, even for numeric indices. To traverse a table in numeric order, use a numerical for loop or ipairs.

The behavior of next is undefined if, during the traversal, you assign any value to a non-existent field in the table. You may, however, modify existing fields. In particular, you may clear existing fields.
m.s: An iterator function for use in for loops.

p.s: The array to be traversed.
The last key that was previously retrieved from a call to next.

r.s: The next key in the table, or nil if the traversal is complete.
The value associated with the returned key.

kid.simple: Gets the next key and value from a table after the one you give it. `pairs` uses it under the hood. A common trick: `next(t) == nil` means the table is empty.
kid.example:
-- Any script
local bag = {}
print(next(bag) == nil) --> true, the bag is empty
bag.apple = 1
print(next(bag)) --> apple 1

m.d: Returns an iterator function, the passed table t, and nil, so that the construction will iterate over all key/value pairs of that table when used in a generic for loop:
m.s: Returns an iterator function and the provided table for use in a `for` loop.

p.s: An array or dictionary table to iterate over.

r.s: The next function as the iterator.
The table t passed as the invariant state.
The initial control value nil.

kid.simple: Used in a `for` loop to go through every key and value in a table, including dictionaries. The order is not guaranteed.
kid.example:
-- Any script
local inventory = { Sword = 1, Potion = 3 }
for itemName, count in pairs(inventory) do
	print(itemName, count)
end

m.d: Calls the function func with the given arguments in protected mode. This means that any error inside func is not propagated; instead, pcall() catches the error and returns a status code. Its first result is the status code (a boolean), which is true if the call succeeds without errors. In such case, pcall() also returns all results from the call, after this first result. In case of any error, pcall() returns false plus the error message.
m.s: Runs the provided function and catches any error it throws, returning the function's success and its results.

p.s: The function to be called in protected mode.
The arguments to send to func when executing.

r.s: true if func executed without errors, false otherwise.
All return values of func on success, or the error message on failure.

kid.simple: Runs a function in 'safe mode'. If the function errors, your script does not crash; instead `pcall` returns false and the error message. If it works, it returns true plus the function's results. Use it for anything that can fail, like data stores and web requests.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local store = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("PlayerCoins")

local ok, result = pcall(function()
	return store:GetAsync("User_1")
end)
if ok then
	print("Loaded:", result)
else
	warn("Failed:", result) -- result is the error message here
end
kid.gotcha: Only the code inside the function is protected. Keep the risky call inside it.

m.d: Receives any number of arguments, and prints their values to the output. print is not intended for formatted output, but only as a quick way to show a value, typically for debugging. For a formatted output, use string.format(). On Roblox, print does not call tostring, but the __tostring metamethod still fires if the table has one.
m.s: Prints all provided values to the output.

p.s: Any number of arguments to be outputted.

kid.simple: Shows values in the Output window. The number one tool for checking what your code is doing. You can give it many values separated by commas.
kid.example:
-- Any script
local coins = 10
print("Hello!")
print("Coins:", coins) --> Coins: 10

m.d:
Checks whether v1 is equal to v2 without invoking the __eq metamethod. The comparison uses primitive equality rules: values of different types are never equal; nil equals only itself; numbers and vectors are compared by value; booleans are compared by value; and all reference types (tables, functions, threads, userdata) are compared by identity (same object in memory).

This is useful when you need to compare two tables or userdata objects that have an __eq metamethod and you want to test whether they are literally the same object rather than semantically equal.

local a = setmetatable({}, {__eq = function() return true end})
local b = setmetatable({}, {__eq = function() return true end})
print(a == b) --> true (metamethod fires)
print(rawequal(a, b)) --> false (different objects)
print(rawequal(a, a)) --> true (same object)
m.s: Returns whether `v1` is equal to `v2`, bypassing their metamethods.

p.s: The first variable to compare.
The second variable to compare.

r.s: true if v1 and v2 are primitively equal without metamethod invocation, false otherwise.

kid.simple: Checks if two values are exactly the same thing, ignoring any custom `==` rules from metatables. Advanced.

m.d:
Gets the real value of table[index] without invoking the __index metamethod. The first argument must be a table; the second can be any non-nil value. If the key does not exist in the table itself, rawget() returns nil rather than walking up the metatable chain.

This is useful for inspecting a table's own stored fields when a metatable-based lookup chain would otherwise intercept the access.

local fallback = {x = 10}
local t = setmetatable({}, {__index = fallback})
print(t.x) --> 10 (found via __index)
print(rawget(t, "x")) --> nil (not in t itself)
t.y = 20
print(rawget(t, "y")) --> 20 (stored directly in t)
m.s: Gets the real value of `table[index]`, bypassing any metamethods.

p.s: The table to be referenced.
The index to get from t.

r.s: The value stored at t[index], or nil if the key does not exist in the table itself.

kid.simple: Reads a value from a table directly, skipping any metatable tricks like `__index`. Advanced.
kid.example:
-- Any script
local defaults = { speed = 16 }
local settings = setmetatable({}, { __index = defaults })
print(settings.speed)          --> 16 (borrowed from defaults)
print(rawget(settings, "speed")) --> nil (not really inside settings)

m.d:
Returns the length of a table or string without invoking the __len metamethod. The argument must be a table or string; passing any other type raises an argument error. For tables, the result is equivalent to what the # operator would return before any metamethod fires; the length of the array portion as determined by the boundary search. For strings, it returns the byte count.

local t = setmetatable({1, 2, 3}, {__len = function() return 999 end})
print(#t) --> 999 (metamethod fires)
print(rawlen(t)) --> 3 (actual array length)
print(rawlen("hello")) --> 5
m.s: Returns the length of the string or table, bypassing any metamethods.

p.s: The table to be referenced.

r.s: The raw length of the table or string without metamethod invocation.

kid.simple: Gets the length of a table or string, skipping any custom `__len` rule. Advanced.
kid.example:
-- Any script
print(rawlen({ 1, 2, 3 })) --> 3
print(rawlen("hello")) --> 5

m.d:
Sets table[index] to value without invoking the __newindex metamethod. The first argument must be a table, the second is the key (must not be nil), and the third is the value to assign. Returns the table itself, which allows chained calls when building tables that have a __newindex guard.

This is the complement of LuaGlobals.rawget() for write operations; use it when you need to bypass a proxy table's write interception.

local log = {}
local proxy = setmetatable({}, {
    __newindex = function(_, k, v)
        table.insert(log, k)
        rawset(proxy, k, v) -- actually store the value
    end
})
rawset(proxy, "x", 42) -- bypasses __newindex; no log entry
proxy.y = 7 -- triggers __newindex; log entry created
print(proxy.x, proxy.y) --> 42  7
print(#log) --> 1 (only "y" was logged)
m.s: Sets the real value of `table[index]`, bypassing any metamethods.

p.s: The table to be referenced.
The index to set in t to a specified value. Must be different from nil.
The value to be set to a specified index in table t.

r.s: The table t that was passed in, allowing chained calls.

kid.simple: Puts a value into a table directly, skipping any `__newindex` metatable trick. Advanced.
kid.example:
-- Any script
local t = setmetatable({}, { __newindex = function() print("blocked!") end })
t.a = 1          --> blocked!
rawset(t, "a", 1) -- really stores it
print(t.a)       --> 1

m.d:
Runs the supplied ModuleScript and returns what the ModuleScript returned (usually a table or a function). If the ModuleScript has not been run yet, it will be executed.

If a string path is provided instead, it is first resolved to a ModuleScript relative to the script that called LuaGlobals.require(), mimicking the Unix-like semantics of Luau's require() expression.

Specifically, require-by-string's resolution semantics are as follows:

  • Paths with the ./ prefix begin resolution at script.Parent.
  • Paths with the ../ prefix begin resolution at script.Parent.Parent.
  • Paths with the @self/ prefix begin resolution at script.
  • Paths with the @game/ prefix begin resolution at game.
  • Each non-prefix component in a given path corresponds to a child instance of the previous component. The exception to this is the .. component, which corresponds to the parent of the previous component.
  • If the desired ModuleScript is not present at the time that LuaGlobals.require() is called, the call will fail and throw an error. In other words, require-by-string is non-blocking: it does not implicitly wait for a ModuleScript to be created.

To illustrate this, each pair of LuaGlobals.require() expressions in the example below contains two functionally equivalent calls. Redundant parentheses have been added to clarify exactly how each path component maps onto an instance.

Once the return object is created by an initial LuaGlobals.require() call of a ModuleScript, future LuaGlobals.require() calls for the same ModuleScript (on the same side of the client-server boundary) will not run the code again. Instead, a reference to the same return object created by the initial LuaGlobals.require() call will be supplied. This behavior allows for the sharing of values across different scripts, as multiple LuaGlobals.require() calls from different scripts will reference the same returned object. If the returned object is a table, any values stored within the table are shared and accessible by any script requiring that ModuleScript.

As noted above, the "object sharing" behavior does not cross the client-server boundary. This means that if a ModuleScript is accessible to both the client and server (such as by being placed in ReplicatedStorage) and LuaGlobals.require() is called from both a LocalScript as well as a Script, the code in the ModuleScript will be run twice, and the LocalScript will receive a distinct return object from the one received by the Script.

Also note that if the ModuleScript the user wants to run has been uploaded to Roblox (with the instance's name being MainModule), it can be loaded by using the LuaGlobals.require() function on the asset ID of the ModuleScript, though only on the server.
m.s: Returns the value that was returned by the given ModuleScript, running it if it has not been run yet.

p.s: The ModuleScript that will be executed to retrieve the return value it provides, or a reference to one (a string path or asset ID).

r.s: What the ModuleScript returned (usually a table or a function).

kid.simple: Runs a ModuleScript and gives you what it returns (usually a table of functions). Runs the module only the first time; later requires on the same side get the same table.
kid.example:
-- ModuleScript named "MathHelpers" in ReplicatedStorage:
-- local MathHelpers = {}
-- function MathHelpers.double(n) return n * 2 end
-- return MathHelpers

-- Script in ServerScriptService
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local MathHelpers = require(ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("MathHelpers"))
print(MathHelpers.double(21)) --> 42
kid.gotcha: The server and each client get their own separate copy of a module. Changing it on one side does not change the other.

m.d:
Returns all arguments after argument number index. If negative, it will return from the end of the argument list.

If the index argument is set to "#", the number of arguments that were passed after it is returned.
m.s: Returns all arguments after the given index.

p.s: The index of the argument to return all arguments after in args. If it's set to "#", the number of arguments that were passed after it is returned.
A tuple of arguments.

r.s: All arguments after position index, or the count of arguments if index is "#".

kid.simple: Picks values from a list of arguments. `select(2, a, b, c)` gives b and c. `select("#", ...)` counts how many there are.
kid.example:
-- Any script
print(select(2, "a", "b", "c"))   --> b c
print(select("#", "a", "b", "c")) --> 3

m.d:
Sets the environment to be used by the given function. f can be a function or a number that specifies the function at that stack level: Level 1 is the function calling setfenv(). setfenv() returns the given function.

If f is 0, then setfenv() changes the environment of the running thread and returns no values.

WARNING: This function allows uncontrolled change of the global/function environment and disables script optimizations. Changes to the environment are not tracked by the script analysis tooling and may result in missing or incorrect warnings.
m.s: Sets the given function's environment.

p.s: Either a function or a number that specifies the function at that stack level.
The function environment table to set for the specified function.

r.s: The function whose environment was set, or no value if f is 0.

m.dep: This function allows uncontrolled change of the global/function environment and disables script optimizations. Changes to the environment are not tracked by the script analysis tooling and may result in missing or incorrect warnings.

kid.simple: Old — don't use it; it slows scripts down. Use ModuleScripts and local variables instead.

m.d: Sets the metatable for the given table t to newMeta. If newMeta is nil, the metatable of t is removed. Finally, this function returns the table t which was passed to it. If t already has a metatable whose __metatable metamethod is set, calling this on t raises an error.
m.s: Sets the given table's metatable.

p.s: The table to set the metatable of.
If nil, the metatable of the given table t is removed. Otherwise, the metatable to set for the given table t.

r.s: The table t that was passed in, with its metatable now set to newMeta.

kid.simple: Gives a table a metatable (secret helper table) that changes how it behaves. Used to make your own object types with shared functions. Returns the same table.

m.d:
Attempts to convert the arg into a number with a specified base to interpret the value in. If it cannot be converted, this function returns nil.

The base may be any integer between 2 and 36, inclusive. In bases above 10, the letter 'A' (in either upper or lower case) represents 10, 'B' represents 11, and so forth, with 'Z' representing 35. In base 10 (the default), the number may have a decimal part, as well as an optional exponent part. In other bases, only unsigned integers are accepted.

If a string begins with 0x and a base is not provided, the 0x is trimmed and the base is assumed to be 16, or hexadecimal.
m.s: Returns the provided value converted to a number, or `nil` if impossible.

p.s: The object to be converted into a number.
The numerical base to convert arg into.

r.s: The numeric value of arg in the given base, or nil if conversion is not possible.

kid.simple: Turns a value into a number if it can. `tonumber("12")` gives 12. If it cannot, you get nil. You can also give a base, like 16 for hex.
kid.example:
-- Any script
print(tonumber("12") + 1) --> 13
print(tonumber("hello")) --> nil
print(tonumber("ff", 16)) --> 255

m.d: Receives an argument of any type and converts it to a string in a reasonable format. For complete control of how numbers are converted, use string.format. If the metatable of e has a __tostring metamethod, then it will be called with e as the only argument and will return the result.
m.s: Returns the provided value converted to a string, or `nil` if impossible.

p.s: The object to be converted into a string.

r.s: A string representation of e, using the __tostring metamethod if available.

kid.simple: Turns any value into text. Useful for joining numbers or nil into a message with `..`.
kid.example:
-- Any script
local score = 99
print("Score: " .. tostring(score)) --> Score: 99
print(tostring(nil)) --> nil

m.d: Returns the type of its only argument, coded as a string. The possible results of this function are "nil" (a string, not the value nil), "number", "string", "boolean", "table", "vector", "function", "thread", "userdata", and "buffer". The buffer and vector primitives are additions from Luau, not from Lua.
m.s: Returns the basic type of the provided object.

p.s: The object to return the type of.

r.s: The basic type name of v as a string (e.g. "number", "string", "table").

kid.simple: Tells you the basic kind of a value as text: "number", "string", "boolean", "table", "function", "nil", "userdata" and a few more. For Roblox things it just says "userdata", so use `typeof` for those.
kid.example:
-- Any script
print(type(5))        --> number
print(type("hi"))     --> string
print(type(workspace)) --> userdata (use typeof to get "Instance")

m.d:
Returns the elements from the given list as separate return values, equivalent to list[i], list[i+1], ..., list[j]. By default, i is 1 and j is the length of list (as defined by the # operator). If the range is empty (i > j), no values are returned. An error is raised if the requested range is too large to fit on the stack.

local t = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}
print(unpack(t)) --> 10  20  30  40  50
print(unpack(t, 2, 4)) --> 20  30  40

-- Common pattern: forwarding a stored argument list
local args = {1, "hello", true}
someFunction(unpack(args))
m.s: Returns all elements from the given list as a tuple.

p.s: The list of elements to be unpacked.
The index of the first element to unpack.
The index of the last element to unpack.

r.s: The elements list[i] through list[j] as separate return values.

kid.simple: Takes the items out of a list and gives them as separate values. `unpack({1, 2, 3})` gives 1, 2, 3. Same as `table.unpack`.
kid.example:
-- Any script
local colors = { 255, 128, 0 }
local c = Color3.fromRGB(unpack(colors))
print(c)

m.d:
This function is similar to LuaGlobals.pcall(), except that you can set a new error handler.

xpcall() calls function f in protected mode, using err as the error handler, and passes a list of arguments. Any error inside f is not propagated; instead, xpcall() catches the error, calls the err function with the original error object, and returns a status code. Its first result is the status code (a boolean), which is true if the call succeeds without errors. In this case, xpcall() also returns all results from the call, after this first result. In case of any error, xpcall() returns false plus the result from err.

Unlike LuaGlobals.pcall(), the err function preserves the stack trace of function f, which can be inspected using debug.info() or debug.traceback().
m.s: Similar to `Global.LuaGlobals.pcall()` except it uses a custom error handler.

p.s: The function to be called in protected mode.
The function to be used as an error handle if xpcall catches an error.
Additional arguments passed to f when it is called.

r.s: true if f executed without errors, false otherwise.
All return values of f on success, or the result of err(errorObject) on failure.

kid.simple: Like `pcall`, but you also give an error handler function that runs when something goes wrong, for example to add extra details to the error.

Lua globals are the built-in functions that come with the Luau language itself, ready to use in any script without `game:GetService`. They include `print` to show messages, `pairs` and `ipairs` for loops, `pcall` to catch errors, `tonumber`/`tostring` to convert values, and `require` to load ModuleScripts.
kid.analogy: Lua globals are like the basic tools that come in every toolbox before you buy anything extra: a hammer (print), a screwdriver (pairs), a measuring tape (type). Every script has them.
whenToUse: Show messages in Output while testing (`print`).
Go through every item in a table (`pairs`, `ipairs`).
Run risky code safely, like data store calls (`pcall`).
Turn text into numbers and back (`tonumber`, `tostring`).
Load shared code from a ModuleScript (`require`).
kid.where: Available everywhere: Scripts, LocalScripts and ModuleScripts. Just type the name, for example `print("hi")`.

terms.global: Something you can use anywhere in any script without getting it first, like `print`.
terms.function: A named set of instructions you can run, like `print("hi")`.
terms.argument: A value you give to a function inside the parentheses. In `print("hi")`, "hi" is the argument.
terms.return: What a function hands back. `tonumber("5")` returns the number 5.
terms.table: Luau's container for many values. A list like `{"a", "b"}` or a dictionary like `{coins = 10}`.
terms.nil: Luau's word for nothing or no value.
terms.error: When something goes wrong and a script stops with a red message in Output.
terms.pcall: Short for 'protected call'. Runs a function and catches errors, so your script keeps going.
terms.iterator / loop: A `for` loop that goes through items one by one. `pairs` and `ipairs` help a loop walk through a table.
terms.metatable: A secret helper table that changes how another table behaves, for example what happens when you add two tables. Advanced.
terms.metamethod: A special function in a metatable, like `__index` or `__tostring`, that Roblox runs in certain situations. Advanced.
terms.ModuleScript: A script that holds shared code. Other scripts load it with `require` and get back what it returns.
terms.Output: The Studio window (View > Output) where `print`, `warn` and errors show up.

examples.title: The everyday globals in one script
examples.code:
local scores = { Ava = 30, Ben = 12 }
local fruits = { "apple", "banana", "cherry" }

-- pairs: every key and value in a dictionary (any order)
for name, score in pairs(scores) do
	print(name, score)
end

-- ipairs: a list in order 1, 2, 3...
for index, fruit in ipairs(fruits) do
	print(index, fruit)
end

-- tonumber / tostring
local typed = "42"
local n = tonumber(typed) -- 42 as a number, or nil if it is not a number
print(n + 1) --> 43
print("Score: " .. tostring(n)) --> Score: 42

-- pcall: catch an error instead of crashing
local ok, message = pcall(function()
	error("Oops!")
end)
print(ok, message) --> false  ...Oops!

-- type: what kind of value is this?
print(type(fruits)) --> table
explain: `pairs` goes through every key/value pair in a table.
`ipairs` goes through a list from 1 upward, in order.
`tonumber` turns text into a number (or nil if it cannot).
`pcall` runs a function safely; if it errors, you get false and the error message instead of a crash.

gotchas: In modern Luau you can loop over a table directly: `for key, value in myTable do`. `pairs`/`ipairs` still work fine.
`tonumber` returns nil for text that is not a number, so check before doing math with it.
`pcall` returns `false` plus the error on failure. Do not ignore the first value.
Use `typeof` (a Roblox global) instead of `type` to tell Roblox types apart, like Vector3 vs Part.

global/RobloxGlobals.d: Roblox provides several unique built-in functions and variables in its embedding of Luau. These are only found on Roblox and are not packaged by default with Luau or Lua.
global/RobloxGlobals.s: Built-in functions and constants unique to Roblox.

m.d: A reference to the Enums data type, which stores all of the available enums that can be used on Roblox.
m.s: Contains all Enum objects.

kid.simple: Holds every Roblox enum: fixed lists of named choices. You use it like `Enum.Material.Grass` or `Enum.KeyCode.Space`.
kid.example:
-- Any script
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Material = Enum.Material.Grass
part.Shape = Enum.PartType.Ball
part.Parent = workspace

m.d: A reference to the DataModel, which is the root Instance of Roblox's parent/child hierarchy.
m.s: Refers to the DataModel singleton, the root instance of a place's hierarchy.

kid.simple: The whole game: the top of the tree that holds Workspace, Players, Lighting and every other service. Mostly used as `game:GetService("Name")`.
kid.example:
-- Any script
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
print(game.PlaceId) -- the ID of this place

m.d: A reference to the Plugin object that represents the plugin being run from this Script. This reference exists only in the context where a script is executed as a plugin and is not passed to ModuleScripts within the plugin. To use this reference in a ModuleScript, you must explicitly pass it.
m.s: Refers to a Plugin singleton when the code is run in the context of a Studio plugin.

kid.simple: Only inside a Studio plugin script: the Plugin object for that plugin, used to make toolbar buttons and more. It is nil in normal game scripts.
kid.example:
-- Script saved as a Studio plugin
local toolbar = plugin:CreateToolbar("My Tools")
local button = toolbar:CreateButton("Hello", "Say hello", "")
button.Click:Connect(function()
	print("Hello from my plugin!")
end)
kid.gotcha: ModuleScripts in your plugin do not get `plugin` automatically; pass it to them.

m.d: A table that is shared across all scripts that share the same execution context level. This serves the exact same purpose as _G.
m.s: A table shared between all code running at the same execution context level.

kid.simple: A shared table, exactly like `_G`: all scripts on the same side can read and write it. ModuleScripts are usually a cleaner way to share.
kid.example:
-- Script A
shared.roundNumber = 1

-- Script B (same side, runs later)
task.wait(1)
print(shared.roundNumber) --> 1

m.d: A reference to the script object that is executing the code you are writing. It can be either a Script, a LocalScript, or a ModuleScript. This variable is not available when executing code from Roblox Studio's command bar.
m.s: A reference to the LuaSourceContainer object (Script, LocalScript, or ModuleScript) that is executing this code.

kid.simple: The script that is running right now. Most often used as `script.Parent` to find the object the script is inside.
kid.example:
-- Script inside a Part
local part = script.Parent
part.BrickColor = BrickColor.new("Bright red")
print(script.Name .. " is inside " .. part.Name)

m.d: A reference to the Workspace service, which contains all of the physical components of a Roblox world.
m.s: A reference to the Workspace service, which contains all of the physical components of a place.

kid.simple: A shortcut to the Workspace service, where all the 3D stuff in your world lives: parts, models and player characters.
kid.example:
-- Any script
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 10, 0)
part.Parent = workspace -- put it into the world
print(workspace.Gravity) --> 196.2 by default

m.d: Schedules a function to be executed after delayTime seconds have passed, without yielding the current thread. This function allows multiple Luau threads to be executed in parallel from the same stack. The delay will have a minimum duration of 29 milliseconds, but this minimum may be higher depending on the target framerate and various throttling conditions. If the delayTime parameter is not specified, the minimum duration will be used.
m.s: Schedules a function to be called on the next Heartbeat after the given duration (in seconds) has passed, with throttling.

p.s: The amount of time that this function will be queued before being executed.
The function that will be executed once delayTime seconds have passed.

m.dep: This method has been superseded by task.delay() and should not be used for future work.

kid.simple: Old — use task.delay instead.

m.d:
Returns the legacy DebuggerManager class which acts as an interface for Roblox's Luau debugger feature.

This function is not recognized by Luau's analysis tool and will raise an undefined global warning.
m.s: Refers to the legacy `DebuggerManager` class which acts as an interface for the Luau debugger feature.

r.s: The DebuggerManager singleton instance.

m.dep: The DebuggerManager is obsolete and serves little to no use case for developers.

kid.simple: Old — no longer useful; use Studio's built-in debugger instead.

m.d: Returns how much time has elapsed since the current instance of Roblox was started. In Roblox Studio, this begins counting up from the moment Roblox Studio starts running, not just when opening a place.
m.s: Returns the amount of time in seconds that the current instance of Roblox has been running for.

r.s: The elapsed time, in seconds, since the current Roblox instance started running.

kid.simple: Old — use time() or os.clock() instead.

m.d: Returns the PluginManager which is a deprecated singleton that was previously required to create plugins. It still has some applicable uses, such as if you need to create a Plugin object from Studio's Command Bar.
m.s: Refers to the `Class.PluginManager`, a deprecated singleton that was previously required to create plugins.

r.s: The PluginManager singleton instance.

kid.simple: An old Studio-only object that was once needed to make plugins. You almost never need it now; plugin scripts get `plugin` directly.
kid.example:
-- Studio Command Bar only (rarely needed)
local p = PluginManager():CreatePlugin()
print(p)
kid.gotcha: Does nothing useful in normal game scripts.

m.d: Prints Current identity is [ID] to the output, where [ID] corresponds to the current thread's security context level.
m.s: Prints "Current identity is X", where X corresponds to the current thread's security context level.

p.s: A custom string to print before the identity number; if omitted, defaults to "Current identity is".

kid.simple: Old — a debugging leftover; you don't need it.

m.d: Returns the GlobalSettings object, which can be used to access the settings objects that are used in Roblox Studio's settings menu.
m.s: Returns the `Class.GlobalSettings` object, which can be used to access settings objects that configure Roblox Studio's behavior.

r.s: The GlobalSettings singleton used to access Roblox Studio's settings objects.

kid.simple: Gives you the GlobalSettings object, which holds Roblox Studio and engine settings like rendering and physics options. Rarely needed in games.
kid.example:
-- Any script
local globalSettings = settings()
print(globalSettings.Rendering.QualityLevel)

m.d:
Runs the specified callback function in a separate thread, without yielding the current thread.

The function will be executed the next time Roblox's Task Scheduler runs an update cycle. This delay will take at least 29 milliseconds but can arbitrarily take longer, depending on the target framerate and various throttling conditions.

The callback function is invoked with two arguments:

  1. The first being the amount of time which elapsed from when spawn was called to when the function was invoked.
  2. The second being equivalent to elapsedTime() or roughly how long the engine has been running.
m.s: Calls a function immediately through the engine scheduler, with throttling.

p.s: The function that will be executed.

m.dep: This method has been superseded by task.spawn() and should not be used for future work.

kid.simple: Old — use task.spawn instead.

m.d: Returns the Stats service. It is preferred that developers use ServiceProvider:GetService() to retrieve it instead.
m.s: Returns the Stats service.

r.s: The Stats service instance.

kid.simple: Old — use game:GetService("Stats") instead.

m.d:
Returns how much time has elapsed, in seconds, since the Unix epoch, on the current local session's computer. The Unix epoch is represented by 00:00:00 on 1 January 1970.

tick() isn't officially deprecated, but has a variety of issues. It can be off by up to one second and returns inconsistent results across time zones and operating systems. Use os.time(), os.clock(), or RobloxGlobals.time() instead. Also consider DateTime.UnixTimestamp and DateTime.UnixTimestampMillis.
m.s: Returns the amount of time in seconds since the Unix epoch according to this device's time.

r.s: The elapsed time, in seconds, since the Unix epoch (January 1, 1970) according to the local device clock.

kid.simple: Gives the number of seconds since January 1, 1970, using this device's clock. It works, but it can be off by up to a second and varies between devices, so `os.time()`, `os.clock()` or `time()` are better choices.
kid.example:
-- Any script
local start = os.clock() -- better than tick() for measuring
task.wait(1)
print("Took", os.clock() - start, "seconds")
print("tick() says:", tick())

m.d:
Returns the amount of time, in seconds, that has elapsed since the current game instance started running. If the current game instance is not running, this will be 0.

If Workspace.AuthorityMode is AuthorityMode.Server, this value is synchronized between client and server.
m.s: Returns the amount of time in seconds that has elapsed since the current game instance started running.

r.s: The elapsed time, in seconds, since the current game instance started running.

kid.simple: How many seconds this game session has been running. Good for timers inside the game.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
task.wait(5)
print("Server has run for about", math.floor(time()), "seconds")

m.d: Returns the type of the object specified, as a string. This function is more accurate than Luau's native type function, as it does not denote Roblox-specific types as userdata.
m.s: Returns the type of the given object as a string, also supporting Roblox-specific types (e.g. Vector3).

p.s: The Luau type that will have its type checked.

r.s: A string representation of the object's type, including Roblox-specific types such as "Vector3" or "CFrame".

kid.simple: Tells you what kind of value something is, including Roblox types like "Vector3", "Color3", "CFrame" and "Instance". Better than `type` for checking values sent by clients.
kid.example:
-- Any script
print(typeof(Vector3.new(1, 2, 3))) --> Vector3
print(typeof(workspace))             --> Instance
print(typeof(5))                     --> number

m.d: Returns the UserSettings object, which is used to read information from the current user's game menu settings.
m.s: Returns the UserSettings object, which is used to read information from the current user's game menu settings.

r.s: The UserSettings singleton instance.

kid.simple: Gives you the UserSettings object, which lets a LocalScript read the player's own game menu settings, like camera sensitivity or graphics quality.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts
local gameSettings = UserSettings():GetService("UserGameSettings")
print("Mouse sensitivity:", gameSettings.MouseSensitivity)

m.d:
Returns the current version of Roblox as a string. The integers in the version string are separated by periods, and each integers represent the following, in order:

  • Generation - The current generation of the application shell that is hosting the client.
  • Version - The current release version of Roblox.
  • Patch - The current patch number for this version of Roblox.
  • Commit - The ID of the last internal commit that was accepted into this version of the client.
m.s: Returns the current version of Roblox as a string, which includes the generation, version, patch and commit.

r.s: A period-separated version string in the format "generation.version.patch.commit".

kid.simple: Old — prints the Roblox version; you don't need it in games.

m.d:
Yields the current thread until the specified amount of seconds have elapsed.

The delay will have a minimum duration of 29 milliseconds, but this minimum may be higher depending on the target framerate and various throttling conditions. If the seconds parameter is not specified, the minimum duration will be used. This function returns:

  • Actual time yielded (in seconds).
  • Total time since the software was initialized (in seconds).
m.s: Yields the current thread until the specified amount of time in seconds have elapsed, with throttling.

p.s: Specifies how long the thread should yield for.

r.s: The actual time yielded, in seconds.
The total time elapsed since the engine started, in seconds.

m.dep: This method has been superseded by task.wait() and should not be used for future work.

kid.simple: Old — use task.wait instead.

m.d: Behaves identically to Luau's print function, except the output is styled as a warning, with yellow text and a timestamp. This function accepts any number of arguments, and will attempt to convert them into strings which will then be joined together with spaces between them.
m.s: Behaves similarly to print, except with more distinct formatting (yellow); intended for messages which describe potential problems.

p.s: This function accepts any number of arguments, and will attempt to convert them into strings which will then be joined together with spaces between them.

kid.simple: Like `print`, but the message shows in yellow (orange) in Output, so warnings stand out. Use it for 'something is not right, but the game keeps going'.
kid.example:
-- Any script
local door = workspace:FindFirstChild("Door")
if not door then
	warn("Door is missing! Check Workspace.")
end

m.d: Legacy function to work around an old task scheduling limitation of LuaGlobals.pcall(); should not be used for new work (use LuaGlobals.pcall() instead).
m.s: Legacy function to work around an old task scheduling limitation of `Global.LuaGlobals.pcall()`.

p.s: The function to be called in protected mode.
Additional arguments to pass to the function.

r.s: Whether the function executed successfully without raising an error.
The return values of the function on success, or the error message on failure.

Roblox globals are built-in names Roblox adds to every script. The most important are `game` (the whole game tree), `workspace` (the 3D world), `script` (the script that is running), `Enum` (lists of fixed options), `typeof` (what kind of thing is this?) and `warn` (print in yellow).
kid.analogy: Roblox globals are like the light switches already built into every room of a house. You do not install them; they are just there, in every script, ready to flip.
whenToUse: Get any service with `game:GetService("Players")`.
Reach parts in the world with `workspace`.
Find things near your script with `script.Parent`.
Pick fixed options like `Enum.Material.Neon`.
Check the type of a value, especially for checking values sent by clients (`typeof`).
kid.where: Available in every Script, LocalScript and ModuleScript. Just type the name.

terms.global: Something you can use anywhere without getting it first.
terms.game / DataModel: The very top of your game's tree. Everything (Workspace, Players, ReplicatedStorage...) lives inside it.
terms.service: A big built-in helper object, like Players or DataStoreService. Get it with `game:GetService("Name")`.
terms.Enum: Short for enumeration: a fixed list of named choices, like `Enum.Material.Wood` or `Enum.KeyCode.E`.
terms.parent: The object something is inside of. If a Script is inside a Part, `script.Parent` is that Part.
terms.Unix epoch: Midnight on January 1, 1970. Many clocks count seconds from that moment.
terms.context level: Which side code runs on. All server Scripts share one; each player's LocalScripts share another.
terms.plugin: A tool that adds features to Roblox Studio, written in Luau.
terms.Output: The Studio window where `print`, `warn` and errors appear.

examples.title: The everyday Roblox globals
examples.place: Script inside a Part in Workspace
examples.code:
-- script: this script. script.Parent: the Part it sits in
local part = script.Parent

-- game: the whole game. Get services from it
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

-- workspace: the 3D world
local baseplate = workspace:FindFirstChild("Baseplate")

-- Enum: fixed lists of options
part.Material = Enum.Material.Neon

-- typeof: what kind of thing is this?
print(typeof(part.Position)) --> Vector3

-- warn: like print, but yellow, for problems
if not baseplate then
	warn("No Baseplate found!")
end

-- time: seconds since this game server started
print("Game has been running for", time(), "seconds")
explain: `script.Parent` finds the Part this script is inside.
`game:GetService` is the safe way to reach any service.
`workspace` is a shortcut to the 3D world.
`Enum.Material.Neon` is one choice from Roblox's fixed list of materials.
`typeof` tells Roblox types apart, which is great for checking values sent from clients.

examples.title: Use typeof to protect a RemoteEvent
examples.place: Script in ServerScriptService, RemoteEvent named PlaceBlock in ReplicatedStorage
examples.code:
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local placeBlock = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("PlaceBlock")

placeBlock.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, position)
	-- An exploiter might send a string, a table, or nothing
	if typeof(position) ~= "Vector3" then
		return
	end
	local block = Instance.new("Part")
	block.Anchored = true
	block.Position = position
	block.Parent = workspace
end)
explain: `type(position)` would just say "userdata" for a Vector3.
`typeof(position)` says exactly "Vector3", so we can reject anything else.

gotchas: Use `task.wait`, `task.spawn` and `task.delay` instead of the old `wait`, `spawn` and `delay`.
Prefer `game:GetService("Workspace")` or `workspace`; both point to the same thing.
`tick()` can be off and differs between devices. Use `os.time()`, `os.clock()` or `time()` instead.
`plugin` only exists inside Studio plugins, not in normal game scripts.
